title: A Scandal at the Center of the Economy
excerpt: Given the obsession over the AI race between the United States and China, you might imagine that news of the man leading the most important company in AI being
body: Given the obsession over the AI race between the United States and China, you might imagine that news of the man leading the most important company in AI being caught in an extramarital relationship with a woman believed to be a Chinese spy would spark outrage and excoriation without parallel
You could suppose that such reckless behavior, upon discovery, might lead to widespread calls for immediate resignation and for deep investigation—not just of the executive, but the entire company

It is curious, then, that, as news came out that the Nvidia CEO, Jensen Huang, had had a romantic relationship with a Chinese businesswoman who was also an asset of Beijing’s Ministry of State Security, notable factions of Silicon Valley and Washington, D.C., seemed nonplussed. “Even incredible humans make mistakes,” Bill Ackman, the billionaire hedge-fund manager, posted on X yesterday. “We should all support him and his family

Onward.” The venture capitalist Shaun Maguire offered a five-point analysis of Huang’s situation, noting that the CEO did something “incredibly dumb” and “bad for America,” but that “my guess is there was no bad intention.” He then argued, “I believe Jensen is irreplaceable for America’s AI leadership.” Elon Musk agreed

From there, the posts, written before we know all the facts of the scandal, got only more absurd , including defending Huang’s affair on the grounds that his kids are adults now. [ Read: America can’t afford an AI recession ] Later in the day, Donald Trump echoed calls for Huang to stay on as CEO

He called Huang “an honorable guy.” The president, who has had extramarital affairs of his own and is credibly accused of sexual crimes by numerous women, sounded unbothered. “I think he probably has an excuse for it,” Trump added
Nvidia’s board of directors seemed equally deferential

It announced an independent investigation into the incident but also stressed that it has “no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised” and that it “has confidence in Jensen and his leadership team.” Huang, for his part, issued a statement yesterday acknowledging the affair and noting that he would cooperate with the investigation
It’s tempting to see this as little more than powerful men defending their kind—a classic example of bros before pressing technological-geopolitical security imperatives
But that explanation misses both Huang’s and Nvidia’s centrality in American politics and the global financial system

Nvidia’s chips are arguably the most important infrastructure component of the AI boom; without the tech, the OpenAIs and Anthropics of the world would be unable to train or power their models—reporting suggests that billionaires have begged Huang for greater allocations of Nvidia chips
This intense demand has made Nvidia a financial juggernaut; in May, its market capitalization was $5.7 trillion, which made it larger than every economy except that of the U.S. and China
Last year, my colleague Matteo Wong and I described the U.S. as an Nvidia-state, much like Saudi Arabia is a petrostate

That’s because, in recent years, the company has become one of the biggest investors of other AI companies; As of July, Nvidia announced that its equity investments valued roughly $99 billion, including in companies such as OpenAI, Anthropic, SpaceX, and data-center providers like CoreWeave

It’s a circular style of investment where companies pay Nvidia enormous sums of money for its chips and then Nvidia reinvests some of that money back into those companies and their competitors, in part so that they can continue to buy chips
You could make a strong case that Nvidia helps support big chunks of the Magnificent Seven ecosystem, the tech companies that are responsible for roughly a third of the S&P 500’s current value

According to The Economist , Nvidia stock has produced “15 cents of every dollar the American stock market has returned since 2023.” Huang, who founded Nvidia in 1993, is the company’s key figure, praised by many in the tech industry as one of the visionaries responsible for the rapid acceleration of artificial intelligence
He’s instrumental in the company’s engineering decisions, its allocation of chips, and other investments
Outside of Silicon Valley, Huang has become a trusted adviser and ally to Trump on AI policy
Huang’s thinking on issues such as AI doomerism (he’s anti-doom) and chip allocation in China (he’s for it—a position that warrants examining, given this weekend’s revelations) influences U.S. policy
This centrality is why one tech analyst on CNBC this morning implied that replacing Huang was a comical suggestion
Huang is a singular figure: the linchpin of the company that is arguably the linchpin of the American economy
Framed another way, Nvidia has much of the financial system in a hostage situation
Which may be why so many people seem motivated to downplay or protect him right now
How else would one describe the prolific excuse-making for him? The information that has come out around Huang’s involvement with the alleged Chinese spy is alarming
Concerns about the relationship have been mounting for more than a year

Alice Huang (no relation to Jensen) worked for the Singaporean data-center company Megaspeed, an Nvidia client the government had been investigating regarding its potential connections to the Chinese government
As The New York Times reported today, Nvidia intervened in the U.S
Department of Commerce’s investigation of Megaspeed; the probe was subsequently halted and transferred to the Justice Department

According to the Times , Trump was briefed about Huang’s relationship roughly a year ago, including the presumption that Alice may be a spy, and “chose not to do anything with that intelligence.” In recent weeks, the Nvidia spokesperson John Rizzo and Huang himself both dismissed claims that the relationship with the woman in question was unusual or romantic in any way—we now know this was untrue

It’s still unclear whether Huang disclosed any pertinent corporate or national-security secrets or whether his relationship with an alleged spy had any impact on Nvidia’s opposition to semiconductor export controls in China
But everything we know so far paints Huang, Nvidia, and government officials in a terrible light, at every turn either ignoring or obfuscating a national-security problem

As more information about the relationship comes out, lawmakers will have to choose whether to take their cues from the markets (Nvidia shares dropped 8.8 percent at one point today—a $400 billion drop in the company’s valuation) or push for more investigation
Trump, who has been reliably motivated in his presidency by the stock market, seems indebted to Nvidia’s performance in the market, as well as to AI investment in general
He’s unlikely to do anything to jeopardize that
Democrats are in a particularly interesting position, fresh off a midterm rout centered on taking a strong stance against tech oligarchs, AI, and data centers and in favor of corporate accountability
Earlier today, Senator Chris Coons said on X that he would push for an investigation into Huang and Nvidia

To press hard on Huang to resign, or to dig deeper into what he and the company knew about the relationship and when, will inevitably risk adding volatility to Nvidia’s share price and, by virtue, the larger Gordian knot of AI investment that is predicated on relentless growth and continued scale
All of this is to say that the moral case regarding Huang is much different from the one that Trump and those with a financial interest in Nvidia’s success will likely consider
This scandal holds an irony that’s especially befitting of the AI moment

title: The End of Stephen Miller’s Recusals
excerpt: S tephen Miller spent his first weekend as White House chief of staff on the patio at Mar-a-Lago, huddling with President Trump and Natalie Harp, his executive
body: S tephen Miller spent his first weekend as White House chief of staff on the patio at Mar-a-Lago, huddling with President Trump and Natalie Harp, his executive assistant, about how to approach the next two years with the House and Senate under Democratic control

Katie Miller—the podcaster, political consultant, and wife of Stephen—spent the weekend in the Washington area, rearranging her own life. “I make every decision based on what’s best for my children and our family,” she wrote yesterday on X, before announcing that she had decided to wind down her podcast
For months, Stephen Miller has recused himself from matters of policy that involve Katie Miller’s other financial interests at the direction of the White House counsel

That meant that Stephen did not work on issues involving the media company Paramount, where his wife had been seeking a podcast deal, or anything to do with space policy or artificial intelligence, because his wife, a longtime adviser to Elon Musk, also worked for SpaceX, the owner of the Grok artificial-intelligence assistant

Katie Miller severed her employment with SpaceX, sold her stock in the company, and forfeited her right to future equity that had not yet vested under her contract, according to a person familiar with the moves
Over the weekend, she also ended a separate contract with Paramount for a planned podcast deal

As a result, a White House official told me this afternoon, “Stephen Miller is no longer subject to any recusals and may fully participate in all meetings and policy matters.” Katie declined to comment

White House lawyers had previously ruled that Katie Miller’s podcast advertising sponsorships from companies seeking official favor from her husband did not require recusals, because sponsorships carry a different ethical significance than consulting arrangements

Sugar-soda boosters at the American Beverage Association, the utility Southern Company, and the Merchants Payments Coalition, a group pushing for legislation to reduce credit-card swipe fees, had all purchased time on her show

But now even those potential conflicts will not be an issue, after a couple more already-recorded episodes from her podcast are released. “Nothing is more important than raising our four kids,” she wrote. “While I’ve loved the podcast, the time commitment is too great and now is the time to step away.” [ Read: A chief of staff who ‘will crack skulls’ ] The Millers met during the first Trump term, when both were working for the administration
Katie Miller later worked as a press secretary and communications director for Vice President Pence, before becoming an adviser to Musk, the founder of SpaceX and CEO of Tesla
During the transition following the 2024 presidential election, Katie Miller worked as an adviser to future Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F
Kennedy Jr., before joining the White House as a special government employee who advised Musk and the Department of Government Efficiency
When she left the White House, she maintained her consulting work for Musk and SpaceX, leading the White House counsel to advise that Stephen Miller recuse himself on related issues

When Katie Miller began working closely with Paramount, offering to help arrange a company party for Trump before the White House Correspondents’ Dinner, Stephen Miller expanded his recusals to cover related issues

Katie Miller’s career change comes amid a public uproar over possible improper influence in the White House, after the former adviser Calley Means went on Joe Rogan’s podcast to allege “demonic” efforts to influence White House policy by lobbyists with close ties to senior officials
Concern about corruption , often focused on the president’s own for-profit efforts in office and the business deals of his children, became a significant issue in the recent midterm elections

Gallup found in September that 89 percent of U.S. adults believed that corruption was widespread in the government, a proportion that had risen 10 points in just one year to the highest level in the two decades that the polling question had been asked

After Trump announced his new chief of staff on Friday afternoon, Katie Miller responded on X: “Watching your best friend and spouse achieve their dreams is a once-in-a-lifetime experience.” She kept the commentary going through the weekend
When Politico published an article about how she had lobbied for the promotion, Miller responded: “BREAKING: Wife supports husband
If your wife doesn’t do this, find a new one.”

title: The Inconvenient Truth at the Center of the Immigration Debate
excerpt: Have liberals learned anything from the border crisis that helped return Donald Trump to office two years ago? Many have not, if a recent report from the Americ
body: Have liberals learned anything from the border crisis that helped return Donald Trump to office two years ago? Many have not, if a recent report from the American Civil Liberties Union is any indication
The group claims to offer a “way forward” for the country’s asylum system, which has become a back door for economic migrants
But the ACLU instead recycles arguments that immigration advocates have made for decades
Too many progressives fail to understand, or acknowledge, the real reason migrants, including those intending to seek asylum, cross the border illegally: People come when they think they can stay
I have been working on border and immigration policy for more than 20 years, serving in senior roles at the White House and the Department of Homeland Security as well as Senate staff
I have seen, up close, surges in illegal immigration under both Democratic and Republican presidents
Again and again, the loudest and most extreme voices have set the immigration agenda for each party, to the detriment of the country

Despite Trump’s concession in yesterday’s 60 Minutes interview that his administration’s handling of immigration was “too tough,” his elevation of the anti-immigration hard-liner Stephen Miller as his chief of staff suggests that this trend will continue
Immigration advocates who deplore the Trump administration’s aggressive tactics have an obligation to propose realistic, constructive alternatives

Yet on the left, the ACLU and other immigration advocates continue to argue that enforcement at the border, including restrictions on asylum eligibility, do not prevent or deter illegal immigration; they simply create pent-up demand and encourage migrants to attempt more dangerous routes

As a result, according to advocacy groups, the only way to stem the tide of illegal immigration is to address the underlying problems that push people to leave their countries, and to provide more legal pathways for these migrants to come to the United States. [ From the November 2026 issue: The babies left behind in America ] In reality, the United States’ inability to promptly remove those who lack a legal basis to remain in the country has been the driving force behind every major surge in illegal immigration since the Obama administration
The U.S. asylum system , created by Congress at the height of the Cold War, presumes that almost everyone who passes an initial screening deserves legal protection

As a result, more than 80 percent of people who claimed asylum at the border from 2014 to 2019 were released into the country, yet immigration judges ultimately granted asylum in less than a fifth of these cases
This legal process can take years, during which seekers are allowed to apply to work, which makes it easy for economic migrants to game the system
Nobody would spend $15,000 in smuggling fees and experience the mortal dangers of the journey north if they didn’t believe that they could stay and get a job
Before 2011, only about 2 percent of people who crossed the border illegally claimed asylum

But as word got out that most people who claim asylum at the border are let in, the percentage of undocumented border crossers who claimed asylum steadily increased , to 16 percent in 2013 and then to 59 percent in 2023––far outstripping the U.S. government’s capacity to process applications in a timely manner
The Obama administration experienced its first surge in migration from Central American families claiming asylum at the border

At the time, advocacy groups persuaded senior officials and key members of Congress to focus on the root causes of illegal immigration—such as violence, corruption, and political instability in other countries—instead of tackling the incentives in the asylum system that encouraged migrants to come here
In 2016, the U.S. invested a record $750 million in aid in projects to create jobs, enhance governance, and improve security in the region
The initiative made modest improvements , but could not fix the problems that were encouraging so many people to flee

What kept illegal border crossings at manageable levels on President Obama’s watch was an increase in border security, a more stringent enforcement of immigration laws within the country, and record-high deportation numbers—for which immigration advocates gave the president the not-so-flattering title of “ Deporter-in-Chief .” At the start of Trump’s first term, the new president’s tough talk about the “invasion” at the border seemed to have deterred some would-be migrants and so further reduced illegal crossings
But migrants soon realized that they could still game America’s asylum system
By 2019 Border Patrol apprehensions along the southwest border exceeded 850,000 , up 115 percent from 2018
Trump’s initial response—to separate the families of asylum seekers at the border—was both ineffective at deterring migration and abhorrent to many Americans

Other restrictions on asylum that his administration introduced in 2019, such as the “Remain in Mexico” program that required asylum seekers to wait in Mexico as their cases played out in U.S. court, had inhumane consequences but did curb border crossings
Emergency measures during the coronavirus pandemic cut the number of crossings even more
But as the pandemic eased, people began moving north again
When President Biden took office in January 2021, illegal crossings had already begun to surge, averaging 70,000 a month from October 2020 through his inauguration
Instead of addressing this problem, Biden spent his first days in office fulfilling campaign promises to immigration advocates
He announced a moratorium on deportations and ended Trump’s asylum restrictions, sending a clear message that the U.S. border was going to be open

He also put Vice President Harris in charge of a strategy to invest more than $5.2 billion in private-sector funds to create more economic opportunities in Central America, which once again did not reduce immigration from the region
Another common argument among immigration advocates is that expanding access to legal immigration will take pressure off the border
The problem is that no realistic amount of legal pathways will satisfy global demand to immigrate to the United States

When I was in the Biden administration, we oversaw the largest expansion of lawful pathways for migrants in a generation, explicitly to reduce illegal immigration from Cuba, Haiti, Nicaragua, and Venezuela
What we found was that illegal crossings dropped only when they triggered clear consequences at the border, such as repatriation of ineligible asylum seekers to Mexico
The United States can and should increase legal pathways for immigrants, but the goal should be to enhance economic growth and reunite families—not to prevent illegal immigration

There is a cruel irony in the fact that, by pushing policies that enable economic migrants to gain entry into the United States via the asylum system, human-rights advocates have encouraged migrants to put their lives at risk on their way to the U.S. border

In 2023, I was part of a delegation to Colombia and Panama to urge those governments to close the Darién Gap —a treacherous and sometimes lethal route between the two countries through which migrants trekked to the United States
From a helicopter, I saw thousands of people streaming out of the jungle after a week-long ordeal

title: Congress vs. Hegseth
excerpt: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube | Overcast | Pocket Casts Back in February, when the United States and Israel first attacked Iran, President
body: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube | Overcast | Pocket Casts Back in February, when the United States and Israel first attacked Iran, President Trump said that it would be a “short-term excursion.” Now, eight months later, as the war with Iran remains without conclusion, the president and his party are dealing with its consequences

As Vice President Vance put it last Tuesday, when Republicans were ousted from their seats in the House and the Senate—not to mention governor’s mansions and statehouses—in a fierce rebuke to the administration’s policies: “The reason we lost is the war.” If voters swung Congress to Democrats in response to the war and its effects, what comes next? Democrats have said that they will vote to end the war; they’ve said, with some Republican support, that they will begin impeachment hearings for Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth

But after naming the hard-line adviser Stephen Miller, the architect and champion of some of the president’s most aggressive domestic and foreign policies, as his chief of staff, Trump may as well double-down on the agenda he’s chased for the past two years

This week on Radio Atlantic , our staff writers Nancy Youssef and Tom Nichols discuss where the administration goes from here, what options exist to get out of Iran, what to make of Hegseth’s potential impeachment, and how the Defense Secretary has changed the relationship between American democracy and the American military
The following is a transcript of the episode: Nancy Youssef: The most enduring impact [Pete] Hegseth has had, in addition to the war, is on personnel

These are people with 20, 30 years experience, and then there’s all the impacts you don’t see—the captains and the majors who are looking at what’s happened to those ahead of them and saying, I’m not gonna stick around
That’s years and years of investment that has been lost, and will take years and years and years to replace
I’m Adam Harris, and today, we need to talk about the war in Iran
Voters cared about the war in this election
An AP poll showed that seven in 10 registered voters wanted to see it end
After Democrats rode a blue wave back to power last Tuesday, Vice President J

Vance wrote on social media, “The reason we lost is the war.” Now Democrats are exploring the legislative tools they have to act as a check on the administration: They have the War Powers Act, they could withhold military funds through appropriations

But as hard-line adviser Stephen Miller takes over as the new White House chief of staff and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth continues to enthusiastically defend his position and the war, the question remains: Where does the administration go from here in a war of their own making? Joining me to discuss are my colleagues Nancy Youssef and Tom Nichols
Harris: Nancy, right after the election, we saw Republicans across the spectrum jump to blaming Iran and the Iran war for their loss

Vance quickly tried to distance himself from the conflict, and then Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth released a video in support of the war, saying: Pete Hegseth: Peace through strength is once again American military policy
Our commander in chief demands it, and so we deliver it

Harris: What does his reaction tell us about the discord within the administration? Youssef: Well, Pete Hegseth was the most vocal advocate of this war, not only internally within the administration, but publicly as well, arguing that this was a just fight, that the United States was stopping Iran from having a nuclear weapon—all without releasing key details about what precisely was happening on the ground or at what cost it was coming to the United States in terms of munitions

And so I think the five-minute video was as much about Iran as it was about threats of an impeachment hearing that Tom Massie put forth before the last session, and Speaker [Mike] Johnson notably relieved Congress so that they wouldn’t have that hearing
There’s at least six charges, some of them related to the war as well as to the boat strikes and some of the other actions that the secretary’s taken
Hegseth: A disgruntled, defeated congressman, along with all his Democrat allies has also dropped sham articles of impeachment against yours truly
Youssef: And so in a weird way, the secretary’s sort of conceding that he faced impeachment by putting out this video and saying that the military needed to come to defense and fight the fight
He didn’t say exactly against whom, but there you go
But he launched a very forceful defense for an impeachment that hasn’t happened yet
But I think more than anybody, he is personally tied to this war because of his advocacy for it

I think if you’re a legislator thinking about impeachment, that video also signaled what he will do if impeached, which is to try to use it as a form of leverage with the president and potentially for his future political career and say that he’s being targeted much in the same way that [Donald] Trump has felt that he got targeted with some of the previous impeachments against him

And so the question becomes, I think, if you’re in Congress, is this the best way to do it, and is this the best time to do it, particularly if the impeachment itself might not lead to a conviction in the Senate? Harris: Tom, we’re seeing this post-midterms shakeup
What does the last week mean for what we can expect out of the White House after the midterms? Nichols: Well, for one thing, the president’s already set the tone: It wasn’t my fault
Had I been on the ballot— which he was, in a way —we would’ve won these things
And so, there’s gonna be a lot of blame-storming going on

Harris: I guess I should say too: What does it mean for the war in Iran? What does it mean for the White House strategy in the war with Iran? Nichols: Well, for the war in Iran, that’s really hard to say because, in theory, Miller has told the president that they have to get out
But that requires Donald Trump admitting a mistake, giving a W to the regime in Tehran, because it will survive and just washing his hands of it
So I suspect that, at least in the short term, it’s gonna be more of what we’re seeing now, that the president acts as if the war is pretty much over
In his interview with Ross Douthat, he said when Ross asked him, What about the strait being closed? And he said, But it’s open
To which, you know, yes, it’s open because there are U.S
Navy ships right now staying there at great expense and a certain amount of risk

And I suspect that you’ll have this kind of phony war going on, where it’s neither peace nor war but it’s to get it out of the public eye and somehow be able to claim what Trump has always wanted to claim
Since the first few weeks of the war, when regime change didn’t happen, what Trump’s really wanted is: Give me a way to say that I won so that I can get out of this thing
And of course that wasn’t helped—I mean, to bring it back to Pete Hegseth—it didn’t help that Pete Hegseth, at least until May, was going out there and saying: We’re killing it
Important to note that it’s been now six months since the Defense Department has bothered to give a press briefing
And I think that’s what to expect from the war

title: Trump Slides Into His Lame-Duck Era
excerpt: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the
body: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture

When President Trump posted on Saturday that he’d asked Dana White, the head of the Ultimate Fighting Championship, to be the new White House press secretary, it felt like a callback to the freewheeling first-term Trump. “I am pleased to announce that the Great Dana White, a violent Fighter and Warrior, has been offered the job of Press Secretary of the United States,” the president wrote on Truth Social , adding that he needed White and his band of mixed-martial-arts fighters “to defend us against the Lunatic Left
Dana will be a Press Secretary like none other

Dana, please take the job!” By weekend’s end, the possibility of the appointment had dissolved, though not without a subplot of speculation that Trump was confusing the impresario with another Dana White who had actually served as a Pentagon spokesperson during his first term
CNN reported that White had declined , and last night, Trump told reporters he never meant it anyway. “I was only kidding, but Dana loves the idea,” he said
Trump has a long record of launching outlandish ideas and then playing them off as jokes when they don’t work out
If it was all a jape, then the weak stab at humor seems to underestimate the electorate’s frustration with his antics
If he was serious and got rejected, it’s even worse
An old maxim goes that when the president of the United States asks you to do something, you do it
But Trump no longer has the juice he did in the early days of this administration, when billionaire tech CEOs were showering him with attention and the odd bauble
Last Tuesday evening, as election results rolled in, my colleague Jonathan Lemire wrote that “Donald J
Trump is now officially, thoroughly a lame duck.” Now we’re getting a glimpse of what that looks like in practice
Start with the cool reception that Trump’s elevation of Stephen Miller to White House chief of staff received among Republicans

Representative Marlin Stutzman called it a “ horrible decision .” Another legislator told Fox News that his reaction was “utter disbelief.” When a Politico reporter informed one member of the choice, they replied , “Please tell me you’re lying to me right now, just to get a reaction.” Take these statements with a grain of salt—Republicans have often been happy to talk trash about Trump anonymously while going along with him publicly—but whether or not they acquiesce with the president matters less now that the GOP is so outnumbered in Congress
One test of where House Republicans actually stand will come this week
Thomas Massie, a renegade GOP member who Trump helped defeat in a primary earlier this year, refiled articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth today

Although Speaker Mike Johnson ( speaking of lame ducks ) had temporarily stymied Massie’s impeachment efforts in September by sending members home until after the midterms, the House is now back in session

Rounding up enough Republican votes to move the articles forward will be difficult but not impossible; a significant number of GOP members lost their seats last week, including many of the more moderate representatives, which means they are less in Trump’s thrall
Assuming that Hegseth is not impeached this month, it seems all but inevitable once Democrats take over
This weekend, presumptive Speaker Hakeem Jeffries said he’s a “hard yes” on impeachment
Republicans’ losses have produced infighting elsewhere in the party too
As Miller moves to take over, fallout from his predecessor Susie Wiles’s tenure continues
Kennedy Jr., appeared on Joe Rogan’s podcast, where he accused Wiles and James Blair , a top Trump political adviser, of selling the MAHA movement out to corporate interests

The Wall Street Journal reports that, ahead of their public social-media fight, Blair texted Means, “If you are gonna try to knife me, I’m happy to return the favor.” Meanwhile Senator Ron Johnson, a hard-right figure from Wisconsin, has picked up on Means’s comments to accuse the Trump administration of “ corruption .” One person in particular left somewhat unmoored by the results is Vice President Vance, who built his entire profile on closeness to a politician whose toxicity is now made plain
In a long post-election X post, Vance pinned the midterm defeat on the Iran war

This was widely seen as a swipe at the president and an attempt to position himself for 2028 , but as The New Yorker ’s Jason Zengerle observed , Vance “didn’t so much throw Trump under the bus as try to bring him on board his bandwagon by essentially putting words in Trump’s mouth.” But Trump does not seem inclined to cooperate
For one thing, he continues to defend the war
On 60 Minutes last night, he acknowledged the political fallout but said, “I think, historically, this will be a very good decision

Is it a good decision for today and tomorrow? Maybe not.” Speaking with reporters last night, he once again declared victory in the unresolved war with Iran and then claimed, falsely and callously, that “we haven’t lost anybody
No soldiers.” At other times, though, Trump has sounded unusually chastened since Election Day
He told The New York Times that he looks forward to working with the Democrats

title: The backlash about data centers might really just be about electricity
excerpt: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI
body: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI
To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here
As voters went to the polls across the US last week, I was in Ashburn, Virginia, part of what’s known as Data Center Alley—the world’s largest data center hub
It’s also where the backlash now sweeping the country arguably first began taking shape
Concrete monolithic buildings loom along every major road, with names like Skybox and CloudHQ
It’s accepted wisdom in Big Tech that the war against data centers must be about something bigger than just data centers themselves

Two days after the midterms, OpenAI’s chief global affairs officer, Chris Lehane, wrote that data centers “have become a proxy for public unease about affordability, corporate power, and people losing control over their futures.” It’s a culture war, in other words
But spending a few days in Data Center Alley left me wondering if it’s really the proxy that Lehane describes
I came away convinced that the data center backlash is more about electricity than Big Tech admits
The industry can improve its image, but it can’t escape the physical consequences of its enormous appetite for electricity
There are two ways to power the sort of data center that AI companies want: connecting to the grid, or generating electricity onsite

In Virginia’s Loudoun County, where data centers are ubiquitous but have been built at a steadier pace than the breakneck expansion now underway elsewhere in the country, most are connected to the existing grid.  One facility I went inside, operated by Equinix, has massive diesel generators onsite for backup but gets its power from the local utility, Dominion Energy
Much of Dominion’s electricity is generated by natural gas (which is cleaner than coal or oil, but worse than renewables)
The average data center operating in this part of Virginia today has a power capacity of 54 megawatts

That’s more than the power draw of the Denver International Airport .  Elena Schlossberg, a prominent activist against data centers in Virginia, told me she’s “always banging my head against the wall” when the industry paints the fight as a culture war. “It was always about power,” she says—that is, electricity
Some Virginia protesters appear more animated by a broader anti-tech populism than Schlossberg, to be fair

But it’s the particular consequences of drawing so much power from the grid that have done the most to shape how the backlash has played out.  Recent protests have led to new rules from the state that data centers must pay fully for the cost of new transmission lines to the grid and make sure they’re not spread among everyone else
Data center developers told me they’re preparing for new rules that would cut them off from grid power during peak demand

Schlossberg also worries about the downstream effects of a strained grid—for example, that data centers will run more diesel generators or that Dominion Energy will expand fossil fuel inputs rather than renewables to meet demand
The overwhelming majority of AI data centers being built elsewhere in the country are not designed this way
The scale desired is so massive that companies are setting up in rural areas where there is virtually no grid infrastructure to connect to
Building there means bringing your own power (so-called “behind the meter” power), in the form of natural-gas-powered turbines
Companies also build diesel generators for backup
Anthropic, for example, has reportedly agreed to pay $3.4 billion for gas turbines in what’s described as the largest power generation purchase by an AI company
Even if grids were nearby, they’d be unlikely to serve the amount of power demanded
The smallest data centers attractive for AI training are 300 megawatts
It’s a lot of power for one industrial site, but not unprecedented: One data center developer told me he’s eyeing a former steel mill already equipped to draw that much electricity from the grid
But the ideal facilities are more like 6,000 megawatts
That’s the estimated draw of the city of Chicago, which is powered by more than 20 power plants within the city alone (and dozens farther out)
The notion of data center companies’ bringing their own power might seem attractive at first, because they wouldn’t be straining the grid

But generating electricity at this scale inevitably affects surrounding communities, and when public utilities build infrastructure of this magnitude, communities have traditionally expected a say in where it goes
Now, private companies are undertaking projects on a similar scale
Natural-gas turbines of any scale release air pollutants
When diesel generators are used, it’s even worse

And in the unprecedented rush to get these facilities operating, companies have become horrible neighbors (recall that Elon Musk violated air quality laws when he set up dozens of turbines to power a data center in Memphis, according to the Environmental Protection Agency)
Big Tech’s tendency to chalk the backlash up to a culture war obfuscates one simple fact: There’s only so pleasant you can make a small city of computers to live around
Sure, companies can pursue better deals that raise tax revenues, hire local workers, and get more community involvement, as the protests are leading them to do

But if a small town is asked to welcome a Walt Disney World, an international airport, a steel plant, and the power plants to run them all, should we be surprised by its trepidation? Again, that’s not to say this is the sole reason for opposition to data centers
Fears of job losses, existential risks, and concentrated corporate power all fuel the backlash, as does misinformation (most facilities use far less water than many people think)
Nor is consuming enormous amounts of electricity inherently bad: Many of the advances that have improved modern life have required just that

title: Nancy Pelosi’s replacement is ready to regulate AI
excerpt: A new voice for AI regulation in Congress: Scott Wiener, who authored the country's first proposed frontier AI legislation, just won Nancy Pelosi's fo
body: A new voice for AI regulation in Congress: Scott Wiener, who authored the country's first proposed frontier AI legislation, just won Nancy Pelosi's former congressional seat and is already pushing for federal action — warning that "we could sleepwalk into a disaster." Recursive self-improvement is keeping him up at night: A recent report suggesting Anthropic may have achieved AI that meaningfully advances itself rattled Wiener, who sees it as proof that Congress is running out of time to act before losing control entirely

He wants regulation with real teeth: Wiener is pushing for a powerful federal AI regulator, whistleblower protections, kill switches, and auditing requirements — and he's firmly against federal laws that would strip states of their own ability to regulate

Cautious optimism, with caveats: Wiener is concerned about Congress's poor track record on tech regulation, wary of Trump's hostility to AI safety concerns, and hoping any crisis that forces action will be, as he puts it, "as small as possible." " data-chronoton-post-id="1148182" data-chronoton-expand-collapse="1" data-chronoton-analytics-enabled="1"> As a California state senator, Scott Wiener authored legislation aimed at curbing the risks of advanced AI

Now, after winning a tight congressional race for former Speaker of the House Nancy Pelosi’s open San Francisco seat, he could play a key role in setting federal AI policy.  I spoke with Wiener on Friday, only a few hours after he had been declared the victor
But he was already thinking about AI risk

The previous day, the AI nonprofit METR had released a report that had been widely interpreted as evidence that Anthropic had achieved recursive self-improvement, a phenomenon in which AI meaningfully contributes to its own advancement and AI progress potentially spins out of control. “It’s very concerning,” Wiener said, citing the report as evidence that we are quickly running out of time to regulate AI. “It was my hope that Congress would take decisive action before [the end of] this year,” he said. “That does not appear to be happening.” Wiener has been increasingly focused on AI in recent years, and he’s made many of the AI safety movement’s concerns his own: During our 20-minute conversation, he used the phrase “recursive self-improvement” half a dozen times, for example.“We need to slow this down,” he says. “Because it’s moving very quickly, and we could sleepwalk into a disaster.” Wiener has already had real influence on AI policy

SB 1047, a bill that he authored in 2024, was set to become the first real piece of frontier AI legislation in the country before it was vetoed by California governor Gavin Newsom; he then sponsored SB 53, a lighter-touch bill that Newsom signed

Both bills have inspired proposed federal legislation.  Wiener’s congressional campaign received over $3 million from Public First Action, a nonprofit in favor of AI regulation that receives substantial funding from Anthropic

That contribution led opponents to criticize him for being too close to the AI industry , but Wiener says that couldn’t be further from the truth.  “Public First supported me because I was the first lawmaker in the country to introduce AI regulation and the first to pass it and get it implemented,” he wrote in a message after our interview. “The attacks on me for [Public First’s] support were shockingly cynical—literally attacking a candidate who actually regulated AI over Big Tech’s objection and falsely claiming the candidate is somehow too close to Big Tech.” Wiener says that if Congress forms a select committee on artificial intelligence—something that Democrats have discussed since September—he’d be eager to serve

And he’s enthusiastic about many of the policy ideas floating around Congress. “I think it’s really important to have a strong, empowered, nimble federal regulator,” he says, noting that Representative Ro Khanna, a fellow Democrat from California, has proposed legislation to establish such a regulator.  He also highlights the importance of whistleblower protections, testing and auditing requirements, and a kill switch requirement, and he wants to see Congress leverage its oversight powers to hold the AI labs to account. “This is about the future of humanity, and we want to make sure that the public has a say and that the public knows what’s going on,” he says

And as a longtime state legislator, he is opposed to broad federal preemption of state AI laws, which some of the proposed federal legislation would require. “States are, as Brandeis says , laboratories,” he notes. “You want the states to be able to continue to be nimble in ways that Congress sometimes is not.” Above all, Wiener says, he wants Congress to pass policies with real teeth. “It’s critically important that when Congress acts, that we do so in a way that is truly meaningful and that meets the moment,” he says

That means taking seriously the possibility of AI catastrophe, something he discusses in the sort of language typically used by AI safety experts. “We’re in a moment that is very dangerous in terms of the risk of loss of control over AI,” he told me. “We need to deal with recursive self-improvement
Once you’re in that realm, that really is potentially a recipe for total loss of control.” He’ll have some allies in the fight against catastrophic AI risk
Senator Bernie Sanders, for instance, has met with many of the AI safety movement’s most influential figures and has spoken repeatedly about AI and existential risk
But there’s still a large gap between Wiener’s Bay Area, AGI-pilled perspective and the national mood on AI, which is anchored by opposition to data centers

The fact that voters approved 40 out of 41 anti-data-center ballot measures on Tuesday might seem to be a good sign for Wiener and others who support AI regulation, but Wiener says he sees this movement as far more tied to local concerns than to bigger questions about AI risk. “Peoople who are really opposed to where AI is going—this is an area where they can actually do something about it,” he says. “But the data center revolt—to me, I think it’s more so that people are upset that there could be something like this in their community, with all the impacts near people’s homes, driving up electric bills and using water

I think that’s the bigger issue for most people, from what I can tell.” Wiener describes himself as only “cautiously optimistic” about Congress’s ability to rein in AI, given its poor track record on regulating the tech industry

He also has concerns about the ability to get legislation past President Donald Trump, who called concerns about catastrophic AI risk a “hoax” in September and has demonstrated a stark unwillingness to collaborate with China, something that Wiener sees as essential to preventing the worst consequences of AI

But he says Trump’s unpredictability provides  some measure of hope, though it’s a fraught kind of hope. “So far what we’ve seen are some problematic things, but not complete disasters,” Wiener says. “I hope that it doesn’t take a disaster to spur the president into acting
And I hope if that’s what it does take—which, like I said, I hope it doesn’t—but if it does, I hope it’s as small as possible.”
quotes: we could sleepwalk into a disaster.

title: Innovating with AI in the special chemicals industry
excerpt: As companies look to accelerate innovation with artificial intelligence, cloud computing, and advanced modeling, the primary challenge is connecting new technol
body: As companies look to accelerate innovation with artificial intelligence, cloud computing, and advanced modeling, the primary challenge is connecting new technologies to reliable data, scientific expertise, and the practical realities of bringing products to market

For specialty chemicals manufacturer Lubrizol, digital transformation is all about giving researchers the tools to test ideas faster, make better-informed decisions, and develop more sustainable materials without compromising performance

Girish Rao, vice president of information technology at Lubrizol, says the company is building a digital foundation that connects business processes, modern data platforms, and cloud infrastructure to support its research and development (R&D) teams
Their goal is to combine decades of accumulated technical data with the deep expertise of chemists and engineers who understand customer needs as well as the physical constraints of their work
Data scientists can help identify patterns, test new hypotheses, and model possibilities before researchers conduct physical experiments

But, Rao emphasizes, “it’s not about replacing scientific judgment; it is about giving our scientists better tools.” Scientists, data scientists, and IT teams approach problems from different perspectives, prioritizing experimental validity, model performance, and platform security and scalability, respectively

By bringing these groups together in “fusion teams,” Lubrizol aligns them around shared objectives, starting with small pilots to build trust. “Once the trust is built between the team members and they know what value they’re about to create,” Rao says, “things go a lot better.” Cloud infrastructure also gives the company flexibility to access computing resources and modern tools without making the substantial investments required to build and maintain its own data centers
These capabilities could prove especially valuable in advancing sustainability
Digital modeling can help researchers evaluate more formulations, explore materials such as starch and corn-based alternatives, and assess trade-offs across a product’s life cycle
Promising a material in a laboratory is only the first step

Scaling production while meeting performance expectations, regulatory requirements, and financial constraints is still a tightrope walk, but AI’s ability to model multiple variables could help teams navigate those competing demands
Looking to the future, Rao expects AI, automation, advanced modeling, digital twins, and connected data to converge as laboratories become more intelligent and manufacturing plants more efficient
The opportunity, he suggests, lies in bringing these capabilities together responsibly and at scale. “It’s not just a single technology

I think it’s the combination of all of these, and it’ll be the ability to connect all these processes that are going to generate tremendous amounts of data.” This webcast is produced in partnership with Infosys

title: The climate case for AI has not been made
excerpt: This week, as countries meet in Antalya, Turkey for the United Nations climate conference, one topic likely to dominate the conversation is artificial intellige
body: This week, as countries meet in Antalya, Turkey for the United Nations climate conference, one topic likely to dominate the conversation is artificial intelligence
The host has already called on countries to commit to ensuring that AI is designed, powered, and deployed in ways that support climate action

But so far, industries around the world aren’t doing nearly enough to harness the technology to actually drive down the greenhouse-gas emissions heating up the planet, despite some very optimistic claims from AI companies

In 2024, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman declared that AI would unleash “astounding triumphs,” including “fixing the climate.” The year before, in a 2023 op-ed , the head of sustainability at Google and her coauthor wrote that AI could reduce global emissions 5% to 10% by 2030.  Some academic researchers have examined these AI-related climate claims

A peer-reviewed study published last year, led by researchers at the London School of Economics’ Grantham Research Institute and the firm Systemiq, estimated that AI could help cut global emissions by the equivalent of 3.2 to 5.4 billion tons of carbon dioxide annually by 2035—roughly on par with the US’s annual energy-related emissions on the high end, even after subtracting AI’s own energy footprint
Those potential gains are mostly concentrated in three sectors: power, meat and dairy, and vehicles
But projections like these are only as good as our willingness to test them against present-day reality

So is there evidence that the largest companies in these three sectors are beginning to integrate AI in line with the study’s projections, and if so, do the results match expectations? Or is the 2035 number still mostly aspirational?  Companies across these sectors have announced plenty of initial efforts to incorporate AI into various business practices

But an AI-assisted review of public information from significant market actors in each sector, conducted and reviewed by the second author of this piece, found that few have announced they’re pursuing the specific emissions-reducing routes that informed the projections in the study—and fewer still claim they’ve used them to achieve meaningful climate progress

The power sector is where the earlier study’s underlying math is most concrete: AI-driven forecasting of supply and demand could increase the amount of renewable electricity that reaches the grid from already-built solar and wind facilities by up to 20%, which could prevent an estimated 1.8 billion tons of emissions a year.  Yet of the grid operators reviewed in China, the United States, and Europe, only one deployed a known meaningful, working AI program of this sort, according to the analysis

A partnership between the UK’s National Grid ESO and Open Climate Fix halved the grid operator’s solar-forecast error (the difference between the amount of incoming sunlight predicted and the amount that actually reaches solar panels), avoiding hundreds of thousands of tons of carbon dioxide a year
Beyond this example in the UK, though, many other grid operators in the EU, the US, and China had little to show in the public record in terms of the AI integration envisioned by the study
The meat and dairy sector offers the starkest contrast between technology readiness and market reality

To achieve the 2035 emission reductions anticipated in the earlier study, AI would need to close the taste and cost gap between traditional proteins and alternative ones, such as lab-grown or plant-based burgers and milk substitutes.  In one of the clearest efforts to achieve this, the AI and food tech company NotCo recently formed a joint venture with Kraft Heinz using its platform Giuseppe , which analyzes plant molecular data to pinpoint combinations replicating the taste, texture, and smell of animal products.  But few other alternative-protein companies had such a deeply integrated way of using AI in product development, the AI-assisted review suggests
Meanwhile, the sector seems to be facing more fundamental problems, including stubbornly slow mainstream consumer adoption and declining funding levels

Most notably, venture capital flowing into cultivated meat fell from a $989 million peak in 2021 to around $83 million last year.  The transportation sector offers some hopeful examples of the type of AI integration necessary to achieve the study’s projections, particularly among battery manufacturers and ride-sharing platforms
CATL—which controls roughly 40% of the global market for electric-vehicle batteries—launched an AI system trained on more than 100,000 battery design cases and 600 terabytes of test data
It cut the time needed to screen candidate materials by two orders of magnitude, according to the company
Independent researchers also found that the ride-sharing platform Didi Chuxing was able cut per-trip emissions 16% on average by using AI-optimized routing to minimize detours

There’s another big problem in the climate case for AI, though: Oil and gas companies are also interested in these tools for many reasons, including the potential to increase production of fossil fuels
Technology firms that committed to sustainability goals in the past should answer questions about how their tools could be used to boost old, dirty energy as well as clean, renewable energy
Finally, it’s also worth noting that integrating AI is just the first step, and it remains unclear to what degree the technology can accelerate the sorts of improvements and innovations envisioned

AI also does little to shorten the standard paths to certifying, permitting, building, packaging, marketing, and selling any resulting products, facilities, or services.  The findings of the analysis, carried out by Anthropic’s Claude Code, were reviewed against public documents and media accounts to ensure their accuracy

It is possible that some companies and utilities in these industries are pursuing AI-assisted applications that would fit into the initial study’s scenarios but haven’t yet been disclosed publicly.  Greater and better-targeted AI integration and efficiency gains in these three sectors may well materialize, bringing the 2035 projections closer to reality
But it won’t happen without deliberate and sustained efforts to ensure that AI delivers more environmental benefits than harms

Notably, so far the rapid adoption of AI models and buildout of data centers has driven a huge increase in energy consumption and emissions, and this has led major tech companies like Microsoft, Google, and others to fall well off track in their corporate climate goals

At this point it would be surprising if the sector even manages to zero out its climate pollution: Emissions associated with global data centers (which may handle AI as well as non-AI computing tasks) could exceed 300 million tons annually in 2035, according to the IEA’s base forecast
Industry leaders must implement the technology in the ways that promise to do the most to drive down emissions
Corporate customers should select models with the lowest environmental impacts and opt to work with the AI developers doing the most to reduce their climate footprint
And states and regions need to do more to incentivize or require all these companies to operate in more responsible ways
Mary Nichols is distinguished counsel at the UCLA School of Law and the former chair of the California Air Resources Board
Jeremy Tamanini is the founder of Dual Citizen, a sustainability research and advisory firm.

    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770820/original/file-20261109-64-c6he2n.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C1%2C8256%2C5503&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">The U.S. Capitol at sunrise, one day after the midterm elections, in Washington, D.C., on Nov. 4, 2026. </span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/view-of-the-us-capitol-at-sunrise-one-day-after-the-midterm-news-photo/2303016391?phrase=u.s.%20capitol%20building&amp;adppopup=true">Roberto Schmidt/AFP via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>There were lots of surprises on the evening of Nov. 3 when the picture of the Democratic midterm success began to be painted on network news touch screens. </p>

<p>The maps kept getting bluer. Eventually, it was clear that this was not an ordinary midterm cycle when the party out of power slaps the wrist of the sitting president and his administration. </p>

<p>It was much bigger than that, something on a scale the U.S. has seen only two times in the past half-century. </p>

<p>One was the <a href="https://www.history.com/this-day-in-history/november-8/the-republican-revolution">Newt Gingrich “revolution”</a> in 1994 that put Republicans in control of the House of Representatives for the first time in 40 years.  </p>

<p>The other was the election of 1974 that flooded Capitol Hill with “Watergate babies” – new members elected just after the Nixon-era scandals.  </p>

<p>In both cases there were high hopes that big changes would take place in the aftermath of remarkable midterm elections. The actual results were more modest than the victors expected.   </p>

<h2>1994’s wipeout election</h2>

<p>The 1994 midterm elections gave the Republican Party a dramatic victory. The Democrats lost their majority in the Senate, and 54 seats were flipped in the House of Representatives, making <a href="https://history.house.gov/People/Detail/13850">Gingrich</a> the first Republican speaker of the House since Eisenhower lived in the White House.  </p>

<p>It was a wipeout election that had not been expected, and it changed the dynamics of Democrat <a href="https://millercenter.org/president/clinton/impact-and-legacy">Bill Clinton’s presidency</a>. </p>

<p><a href="https://www.npr.org/2018/11/01/662906525/combative-tribal-angry-newt-gingrich-set-the-stage-for-trump-journalist-says">The combative Gingrich</a> emerged as a political celebrity; partisanship intensified and gridlock became the new norm.  Confrontations over spending led to controversial <a href="https://millercenter.org/1995-96-government-shutdown">government shutdowns</a> and the first modern threat to <a href="https://www.npr.org/2019/01/12/683304824/the-longest-government-shutdown-in-history-no-longer-how-1995-changed-everything">default on America’s debt obligations</a>. </p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/lyqrNg5XOJc?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">A 1994 Newt Gingrich interview with CBS News on Republican victories and the 1994 Contract with America.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Because the new Republican congressional majorities appeared to overreach in their efforts to cut taxes and spending, <a href="https://www.brookings.edu/articles/governing-in-an-age-of-no-majorities-bill-clintons-mission-for-a-second-term/">Clinton was able to recover sufficient popularity</a> to win a second term.  </p>

<p>In the run-up to his bid for reelection, <a href="https://www.politico.com/story/2007/01/clintons-state-of-union-helped-turn-around-loss-of-congress-002416">Clinton took the electoral rebuke of 1994 to heart</a> and followed a centrist strategy that represented a move to the right of longtime Democratic positions on welfare, crime and immigration. He continued to oppose many Republican policy proposals but worked with Republicans to craft <a href="https://cosm.aei.org/lessons-from-the-1996-welfare-reform-law-approaching-its-30th-anniversary/">welfare reform legislation</a> and new bills dealing with <a href="https://www.presidency.ucsb.edu/documents/remarks-signing-the-violent-crime-control-and-law-enforcement-act-1994">crime</a> and <a href="https://www.presidency.ucsb.edu/documents/the-presidents-radio-address-317">immigration</a>. Budget confrontation eventually gave way to compromise, and for a few years in the late 1990s <a href="https://www.brookings.edu/articles/how-did-the-budget-get-balanced-in-the-late-1990s/">the United States had a balanced budget</a>. </p>

<p>Partisanship became more personal in Clinton’s second term when <a href="https://millercenter.org/the-presidency/impeachment/clinton-impeachment-and-its-fallout">Gingrich pushed for impeachment</a> following the revelations of the president’s affair with Monica Lewinsky.  </p>

<p>Clinton, with a tarnished reputation, <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/world/1999/feb/12/clinton.usa2">survived his Senate trial</a>. Ironically, it was <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/1998/11/07/us/the-speaker-steps-down-the-career-the-fall-of-gingrich-an-irony-in-an-odd-year.html">Gingrich who resigned</a> after failing to remove the president at the ballot box or in the impeachment process. </p>

<p>Gingrich, the biggest winner in the 1994 midterms, left office with a promised revolution largely unrealized. </p>

<h2>1974’s Watergate reformers</h2>

<p>Going back even further in American political history, the midterm elections following President <a href="https://www.gilderlehrman.org/sites/default/files/2024-12/GLI_Resignation%20Speech%20Nixon_2024_printer.pdf">Richard Nixon’s resignation after the Watergate scandal</a> produced a Democratic Party victory.  </p>

<p>That victory was not a surprise; the scale of it was.  </p>

<p>Democrats, who already had majorities in the House and Senate, <a href="https://www.politico.com/magazine/story/2014/11/the-democrats-high-water-mark-came-40-years-ago-112492">won a huge margin in the congressional popular vote</a> and brought new members to both chambers <a href="https://www.politico.com/magazine/story/2018/05/26/congress-broke-american-politics-218544/">who were younger, more liberal</a> and <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2019/01/03/opinion/house-democrats-watergate-1974.html">reform-minded</a>.   </p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770848/original/file-20261109-64-fd9rn1.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A newspaper front page from Nov. 6, 1974 with a huge headline about how the 'DEMOCRATS PILE UP CONGRESS GAINS.'" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770848/original/file-20261109-64-fd9rn1.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770848/original/file-20261109-64-fd9rn1.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=470&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770848/original/file-20261109-64-fd9rn1.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=470&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770848/original/file-20261109-64-fd9rn1.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=470&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770848/original/file-20261109-64-fd9rn1.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=590&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770848/original/file-20261109-64-fd9rn1.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=590&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770848/original/file-20261109-64-fd9rn1.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=590&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">The front page of The New York Times on the day after the 1974 midterm elections.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://timesmachine.nytimes.com/timesmachine/1974/11/06/issue.html">New York Times Archive</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>They wanted to prevent future Watergates. New laws would make the <a href="https://responsiblestatecraft.org/watergate-babies-midterms/">government more open, more honest and more accountable</a>. New and more staff would allow Congress to be less reliant on executive branch information and better able to act in foreign policy and budget management. Special prosecutors would be appointed to investigate abuses of power and violations of law. </p>

<p>A Democrat, Jimmy Carter, <a href="https://www.270towin.com/1976-election/">would be elected president</a> two years after the massive 1974 midterm victory, and more reform legislation would be passed. </p>

<p>The <a href="https://www.aei.org/events/watergate-revisited-the-reforms-and-the-reality-40-years-later/">post-Watergate congressional agenda was long and bold</a> – the war powers resolution, a freedom of information act, the creation of inspectors general, campaign finance reform, a presidential records act and new legislation to regulate foreign intelligence surveillance and the bribing of foreign officials.  </p>

<p>These new laws were supposed to stop, or uncover, the kind of wrongdoing that made Nixon an <a href="https://www.govexec.com/federal-news/2006/02/imperial-presidency-has-long-history/21214/">imperial president</a>. </p>

<p>The new laws and institutions certainly made a difference – <a href="https://hls.harvard.edu/today/watergate-era-reforms-50-years-later/">but not without creating their own problems</a>.</p>

<p>All the post-Watergate presidents thought <a href="https://dornsife.usc.edu/scribe/2026/09/18/is-the-war-powers-resolution-constitutional/">the war powers resolution was unconstitutional</a>, objecting to its  restrictions on the president’s authority as commander in chief, and <a href="https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R42738">U.S. military interventions overseas continued to occur</a>. Special prosecutors <a href="https://www.washingtonpost.com/history/2019/03/19/whiskey-watergate-whitewater-how-special-prosecutor-robert-muellers-predecessors-made-history/">conducted many investigations</a>, but often at great expense and without adequate supervision or meaningful results.  </p>

<p>Carter, narrowly elected president in 1976, served only one term and <a href="https://www.270towin.com/1980-election/">lost reelection to Ronald Reagan</a>, who fully restored the Republican Party’s dominance in presidential politics. </p>

<p>Over time, many presidents, <a href="https://www.opb.org/article/2025/02/15/trumps-efforts-with-doge-cuts-test-watergate-era-reforms/">especially Donald Trump</a>, dismantled or ignored important elements of the post-Watergate reforms.   </p>

<p>The large and enthusiastic congressional majorities that took power after the 1974 midterms were energetic but produced <a href="https://www.politico.com/magazine/story/2018/05/26/congress-broke-american-politics-218544/">a political legacy with complicated and controversial results</a>. </p>

<h2>Chaos and conflict – or compromise?</h2>

<p>What is the country likely to see in the next few months and the next two years?  </p>

<p>Will it be chaos, conflict and occasional compromise, like the politics that followed the midterms in 1994? Or will it be earnest and sometimes heavy-handed congressional efforts to investigate and prevent presidential wrongdoing, like those that swept through Washington after 1974?</p>

<p>Surprising midterm elections that create new majorities on Capitol Hill look to be revolutions in the days after they occur. Years later, they often appear to be more complex – and less significant.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/296034/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

<title>New blood test claims to detect 50-plus cancers before symptoms – but there’s no evidence it can reduce your risk of dying from cancer</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/768896/original/file-20261028-52-jdeq4j.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C2121%2C1414&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">While a blood test may be relatively safe, the consequences of its results can be far riskier.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/medical-lab-technician-hold-sample-blood-for-royalty-free-image/638947606">Douglas Sacha/Moment</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Cancer isn’t the <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/fastats/leading-causes-of-death.htm">leading cause of death in the United States</a>; heart disease ranks first in that regard. But it’s cancer that strikes fear into the hearts of many Americans. </p>

<p>Cancer can take an excruciating toll on its <a href="https://doi.org/10.3322/caac.70043">millions of victims</a> and their family members. Cancer treatments are often highly toxic, and the disease is increasingly <a href="https://theconversation.com/colon-cancer-rates-are-rising-in-young-americans-but-insurance-barriers-are-making-screening-harder-228673">striking people</a> <a href="https://theconversation.com/pope-leo-xivs-lung-cancer-highlights-growing-number-of-nonsmokers-diagnosed-with-the-disease-and-younger-people-too-294348">at younger ages</a>, which is why it accounts for <a href="https://doi.org/10.2105/AJPH.2017.303986">more years of potential life lost</a> than heart disease.</p>

<p>So when a blood test comes along that claims to be able to screen for over 50 cancers at once in a single blood draw before symptoms appear – as is the case for the <a href="https://www.nhs-galleri.org/">Galleri test</a>, by the biotech company GRAIL – it might seem like society has a Holy Grail of modern medicine at their fingertips.</p>

<p>But a closer look at the evidence suggests that the Galleri test is not yet the universal screening breakthrough patients and doctors hope for.</p>

<p>As a physician who <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=qgDmAewAAAAJ&amp;hl=en">studies early cancer detection</a>, and as chair of the <a href="https://www.cancer.org/health-care-professionals/american-cancer-society-prevention-early-detection-guidelines/overview/cancer-screening-guideline-development-group.html">American Cancer Society’s screening guideline development group</a>, I have been following this test’s development with interest.</p>

<p>While the Galleri test certainly shows great promise, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2505723">clinical trial data</a> indicates that it struggles with early-stage cancer detection and has not yet been shown to lower the risk of death from cancer or prevent advanced cancer. Across all cancer stages, the test missed over two-thirds of cancer cases.</p>

<p>On Sept. 23, 2026, an advisory panel to the U.S. Food and Drug Administration <a href="https://www.fda.gov/advisory-committees/advisory-committee-calendar/september-23-2026-molecular-and-clinical-genetics-panel-medical-devices-advisory-committee-meeting">voted to recommend approval</a> of the Galleri test. While a recommendation from the FDA’s advisory panel is not the same as full approval from the agency, it marks a critical first step in the process of potentially making the test widely available to the American public. The FDA has <a href="https://www.beckersoncology.com/pharmacy/fda-panel-backs-first-multi-cancer-blood-test-what-to-know/">not yet announced</a> when it will make a decision on the test.</p>

<p>But even as the advisory panel approved the test, panelists recommended that the word “early” be removed from “early cancer detection test” in product labeling. Panel members were not convinced the test can find cancers at their earliest and most curable stages, and they expressed uncertainty about the test’s benefit to patients at this time.</p>

<p>Given this uncertainty, careful scrutiny of the data behind the test can help doctors and patients make informed decisions about whether to use it.</p>

<h2>What is the Galleri test? How does it work?</h2>

<p>Galleri is part of an emerging class of <a href="https://theconversation.com/a-blood-test-that-screens-for-multiple-cancers-at-once-promises-to-boost-early-detection-191728">multicancer early detection tests</a>. These tests do not diagnose cancer: If a test is positive, further evaluation is necessary to determine whether cancer is present, and, if so, what type of cancer. It is offered as a screening test, similar to mammography for breast cancer screening or PSA testing for prostate cancer screening, but with the potential advantage of screening for many cancers at once, including many for which no screening test currently exists.</p>

<p>The Galleri test looks for DNA fragments in blood that are associated with cancer. When something goes wrong with your DNA, whether because you inherited a mutation or something in your environment triggered that mutation, the processes that regulate cell division can go awry. Uncontrolled cell division can trigger the growth of cancer cells.</p>

<p>Galleri and other multicancer early detection tests in development look for differences that distinguish the DNA produced by tumor cells from normal cells. Galleri <a href="https://theconversation.com/a-blood-test-that-screens-for-multiple-cancers-at-once-promises-to-boost-early-detection-191728">identifies unique tags</a> on cancer DNA called methylation markers and uses machine learning algorithms to generate a positive or negative test result. </p>

<h2>What are the strengths of the Galleri test?</h2>

<p>The Galleri test looks for DNA signals from <a href="https://doi.org/10.1038/s41591-025-04093-9">over 50 cancers</a>, including the 12 that account for almost <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.annonc.2020.02.011">two-thirds of cancer deaths in the U.S</a>, such as lung and pancreas cancer. Importantly, it provides information on which organ the possible tumor likely originated from. Currently recommended cancer screenings are largely <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/cancer/prevention/screening.html">limited to four types</a> of cancer.</p>

<p>Many of the cancers the Galleri test looks for are not currently included in routine screening. Moreover, the test has a very low false positive rate: Only about <a href="https://doi.org/10.1038/s41591-026-04652-8">0.5% of people who get the test</a> are incorrectly identified as having cancer, or one person out of every 200 tests. A <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.amjmed.2025.10.013">false positive rate</a> is the percentage of people who are told they have cancer but actually don’t. This requires that patients get more testing, which can be costly, sometimes risky and often worrisome.</p>

<p>In comparison, many currently recommended screening tests, such as the Cologuard stool test for colorectal cancer, have <a href="https://doi.org/10.3322/caac.70083">false positive rates in the 10% range</a>. </p>
