            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Colonoscopies are more cumbersome than a blood draw, but they are effective at detecting cancer.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/doctor-explaining-colonoscopy-results-to-patient-royalty-free-image/2217548501">Halfpoint/iStock via Getty Images Plus</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>This very low false positive rate also translates into another strength – a very high <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/978-981-99-9283-6_2196">positive predictive value, or PPV</a>, which is the probability that a positive test result actually means cancer is present. The PPV of the Galleri test was <a href="https://doi.org/10.1038/s41591-026-04652-8">52% across three annual screens</a>, meaning over half the positive results actually led to a cancer diagnosis. This is good because it gives people confidence that the test is more than 50% correct.</p>

<p>For context, the PPVs of most recommended screening tests – such as <a href="https://doi.org/10.3322/caac.70083">stool tests</a> for colorectal cancer, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/s10549-023-07124-6#citeas">mammography</a> for breast cancer, or the <a href="https://doi.org/10.1186/s12916-021-02026-0">HPV test</a> for cervical cancer – are typically below 10%, meaning most positive results don’t lead to a cancer diagnosis.</p>

<p>The Galleri test also can predict with high accuracy where a cancer originated in the body. In one study of 32,000 U.S. adults age 50 and older who received a Galleri blood test, cancer was diagnosed in about <a href="https://doi.org/10.1038/s41591-026-04618-w">0.5% of them – 173 patients</a>. Of these patients, the test correctly predicted the cancer type in 91%. This specificity could help clinicians select more targeted evaluations rather than looking for cancer anywhere in the body. </p>

<h2>What are the limitations of the Galleri test?</h2>

<p>Despite these impressive results, the Galleri test has several major shortcomings. </p>

<p>For one, the test is not as good at detecting cancer in its earliest stages as currently recommended screening tests, which is the main point of a cancer screening test. The test’s ability to detect cancer at all stages was less than 31% over three annual rounds of screening, meaning the test <a href="https://doi.org/10.1038/s41591-026-04652-8">missed 69% of cases</a>. Of the cancers detected in the study, comparing outcomes from getting the Galleri test three years in a row to routine cancer screening, 60% of the cancers detected in the people who got the Galleri test were early stage, which was almost identical to those who didn’t get it.</p>

<p>In addition, the Galleri test did not perform any better than standard screening tests at detecting cancer early. The detection rate for early-stage cancers was only <a href="https://doi.org/10.1038/s41591-026-04652-8">21% over three years of screening</a>, meaning almost 80% were missed. Cancer is <a href="https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2022.11744">most curable in its early stages</a>, so this shortcoming is a major one. Such a low detection rate can lead to <a href="https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.281.21.2029">false reassurance</a> from an incorrectly negative test result. </p>

<p>Perhaps the most important shortcoming of the Galleri test is that it hasn’t yet proved that it can save lives or even reduce the risk of being diagnosed with late-stage cancer. The main goal of the trial was to show that the test could reduce the incidence of late-stage cancers over three years of screening – and it <a href="https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2505723">failed to do so</a>. In other words, one of the hopes was that the test could reduce the risk of being diagnosed with advanced cancer by finding and treating cancer early – but as of now, there is no evidence to support this. </p>

<p>There was a hint that the incidence of Stage 4 cancer was trending lower by the third year of screening. But more time is needed to determine whether this is a true finding and, if so, whether it leads to a lower risk of dying from cancer.</p>

<p>Requests for comment from GRAIL were not returned.</p>

<h2>What did the FDA’s panel recommend?</h2>

<p>The FDA advisory panel <a href="https://www.fda.gov/media/195032/download">took three votes</a>. While one of of these votes followed the evidence, two of them were surprisingly counterintuitive.</p>

<p>First, the panel voted 10-0 to recommend that the Galleri test is safe. While undergoing a blood test doesn’t typically involve any substantive risk, a positive result may prompt further testing, such as biopsies, that are riskier than a blood test and can incur additional costs.</p>

<p>These harms can be particularly hard to swallow if the test turns out to be a false alarm, as it will in about half of cases. One study evaluating Galleri’s safety found that 0.6% of those who had the test ended up <a href="https://doi.org/10.1038/s41591-026-04618-w">undergoing an invasive diagnostic procedure</a>, but none experienced serious complications. Hence, the safety vote appears to have been warranted.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/768909/original/file-20261028-52-rke1tb.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Patient and clinician clasping hands" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/768909/original/file-20261028-52-rke1tb.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/768909/original/file-20261028-52-rke1tb.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=306&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/768909/original/file-20261028-52-rke1tb.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=306&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/768909/original/file-20261028-52-rke1tb.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=306&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/768909/original/file-20261028-52-rke1tb.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=385&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/768909/original/file-20261028-52-rke1tb.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=385&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/768909/original/file-20261028-52-rke1tb.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=385&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Catching cancer early is critical to potentially curing it.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/healthy-lifestyle-and-medical-concept-royalty-free-image/2215511952">seb_ra/iStock via Getty Images Plus</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Second, the panel voted 6-4 to recommend that the test is effective, though a number of the panelists cast their yes vote on the condition that the company remove the term “early” from the label “multi-cancer early detection” test. </p>

<p>This outcome, however, does not have the evidence to back it up. Available studies indicate the Galleri test does not reduce the incidence of late-stage cancer and performs poorly in detecting early-stage cancer. Additionally, there is no evidence that it lowers the risk of dying from cancer. </p>

<p>Finally, the panel voted 7-2 with one abstention to recommend that the benefits of the Galleri test outweigh the risk. But if there is no proven benefit to the test, how can the benefits outweigh the risks, even if the risk is low? </p>

<p>While the advisory panel acknowledged the test’s serious limitations, it still went ahead and recommended approval. One of the panel members stated that the ability to find more early-stage cancers in a broader population is a benefit, even though that hasn’t been proved yet. “So perhaps my ‘yes’ is a hopeful (vote) rather than an accurate one,” said the panel member.</p>

<p>The problem is that “hope” does not reduce death and disability from cancer.  </p>

<h2>Should you get the Galleri test or not?</h2>

<p>If the FDA agrees with its advisory panel’s recommendation and approves the Galleri test, it will likely be more widely marketed to the American public. Regardless, there remain many caveats, and I believe patients will want to be cautious.</p>

<p>First, FDA approval does not guarantee insurance coverage. The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services has a <a href="https://doi.org/10.1001/jamainternmed.2023.3961">separate coverage determination process</a>, and it is not required to grant coverage to FDA-approved tests. The out-of-pocket cost of the Galleri test is <a href="https://web.archive.org/web/20261002115431/https://www.galleri.com/patient/faqs#tab-448492-448507">currently US$949</a>. </p>

<p>It remains unclear whether the test can reduce your risk of dying from cancer or being diagnosed with advanced cancer. However, if you’re willing to pay the annual cost of the test, are willing to undergo further testing despite a high rate of false alarms, and are not overly reassured by a falsely negative test result, you can ask your doctor for more information about the test.</p>

<p>What doctors and researchers are certain about is the importance of staying up to date with <a href="https://doi.org/10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2023.44698">currently recommended cancer screening tests</a> for colon, breast, cervical and lung cancers, even if you decide to get the Galleri test. These tests are proven to detect early-stage cancer and lower your risk of dying from cancer. That’s the bottom line.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/293409/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

Douglas Sacha/Moment Cancer isn’t the leading cause of death in the United States ; heart disease ranks first in that regard
But it’s cancer that strikes fear into the hearts of many Americans
Cancer can take an excruciating toll on its millions of victims and their family members
Cancer treatments are often highly toxic, and the disease is increasingly striking people at younger ages , which is why it accounts for more years of potential life lost than heart disease

So when a blood test comes along that claims to be able to screen for over 50 cancers at once in a single blood draw before symptoms appear – as is the case for the Galleri test , by the biotech company GRAIL – it might seem like society has a Holy Grail of modern medicine at their fingertips
But a closer look at the evidence suggests that the Galleri test is not yet the universal screening breakthrough patients and doctors hope for
As a physician who studies early cancer detection , and as chair of the American Cancer Society’s screening guideline development group , I have been following this test’s development with interest

While the Galleri test certainly shows great promise, clinical trial data indicates that it struggles with early-stage cancer detection and has not yet been shown to lower the risk of death from cancer or prevent advanced cancer
Across all cancer stages, the test missed over two-thirds of cancer cases
On Sept. 23, 2026, an advisory panel to the U.S
Food and Drug Administration voted to recommend approval of the Galleri test

While a recommendation from the FDA’s advisory panel is not the same as full approval from the agency, it marks a critical first step in the process of potentially making the test widely available to the American public
The FDA has not yet announced when it will make a decision on the test
But even as the advisory panel approved the test, panelists recommended that the word “early” be removed from “early cancer detection test” in product labeling
Panel members were not convinced the test can find cancers at their earliest and most curable stages, and they expressed uncertainty about the test’s benefit to patients at this time
Given this uncertainty, careful scrutiny of the data behind the test can help doctors and patients make informed decisions about whether to use it

These tests do not diagnose cancer: If a test is positive, further evaluation is necessary to determine whether cancer is present, and, if so, what type of cancer

It is offered as a screening test, similar to mammography for breast cancer screening or PSA testing for prostate cancer screening, but with the potential advantage of screening for many cancers at once, including many for which no screening test currently exists
The Galleri test looks for DNA fragments in blood that are associated with cancer
When something goes wrong with your DNA, whether because you inherited a mutation or something in your environment triggered that mutation, the processes that regulate cell division can go awry
Uncontrolled cell division can trigger the growth of cancer cells
Galleri and other multicancer early detection tests in development look for differences that distinguish the DNA produced by tumor cells from normal cells
Galleri identifies unique tags on cancer DNA called methylation markers and uses machine learning algorithms to generate a positive or negative test result

Importantly, it provides information on which organ the possible tumor likely originated from
Currently recommended cancer screenings are largely limited to four types of cancer
Many of the cancers the Galleri test looks for are not currently included in routine screening
Moreover, the test has a very low false positive rate: Only about 0.5% of people who get the test are incorrectly identified as having cancer, or one person out of every 200 tests
A false positive rate is the percentage of people who are told they have cancer but actually don’t
This requires that patients get more testing, which can be costly, sometimes risky and often worrisome

<title>Paraguay’s bank collapse brought down a president – and exposed as myth the nation’s status as a ‘Dubai of South America’</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770644/original/file-20261108-64-pkt68g.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C1023%2C682&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Protesters on Nov. 5 burn a effigy depicting now ex-President Santiago Pena outside Congress in Asuncion, Paraguay, days after the beginning of a banking crisis to which he was linked. 
 </span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/Paraguay%20Bank%20Failure/c6ea16935d8947669adf6852ec0085a6/photo">AP Photo/Jorge Saenz</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>It started on Nov. 3, 2026, when millions of Paraguayans trying to access the Ueno banking app found they <a href="https://www.reuters.com/business/finance/what-is-ueno-bank-how-did-it-trigger-paraguays-political-crisis-2026-11-05/">could no longer get their money</a>. In a matter of days, the financial situation escalated into political crisis, in which the country’s president was ousted, placed under house arrest and <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/06/world/americas/paraguay-president-removed-ueno.html">charged with several corruption-related</a> crimes.   </p>

<p>The political and financial crisis exposes a central contradiction in Paraguay’s <a href="https://www.worldbank.org/ext/en/country/paraguay">recent economic development</a>. Ueno, a bank celebrated for expanding financial access to ordinary Paraguayans, grew through unusually close relationships with political elites and public institutions. And while the Ueno crisis came as a shock, there were clear warning signs. </p>

<p>As scholars with expertise in various aspects of Paraguay’s contemporary <a href="https://nacla.org/paraguay-operation-condor-disappearance/">political</a>, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/03066150.2017.1384726">economic and environment development</a>, we believe the collapse raises troubling questions about who benefits from financial modernization, who controls it and who bears the risks when it fails. The political relationships through which financial institutions grow, regulators exercise authority and public resources are entrusted to private companies are crucial national concerns, especially in a country that has presented itself internationally as a model of economic stability. </p>

<h2>A bank that grew faster than scrutiny</h2>

<p>Founded as a digital lender in 2021, Ueno attracted customers with mobile banking and cash-back offers. Its expansion <a href="https://www.forbesargentina.com/negocios/ueno-querer-ser-primer-unicornio-paraguayo-una-crisis-bancaria-hizo-renunciar-pena-n101802">brought useful services</a> to people underserved by conventional banks, including rural customers. Ueno also <a href="https://www.abc.com.py/economia/2025/04/13/evolucion-de-tarjetas-de-credito-en-el-sistema-bancario-paraguayo/">expanded the credit card market to low-income customers</a>, an unprecedented move compared to previously restricted banking practices. </p>

<p>As Ueno expanded, Paraguay <a href="https://www.bloomberg.com/news/features/2026-03-20/paraguay-why-a-little-known-trump-ally-is-attracting-investor-money">increasingly attracted investors</a> drawn by its low taxes, economic stability and business-friendly policies. Promoted by some as a “<a href="https://infonegocios.com.py/y-ademas/paraguay-tiene-el-potencial-de-convertirse-en-el-dubai-de-sudamerica-segun-referente-extranjero">Dubai of South America</a>,” the country also became a magnet for <a href="https://elsurti.com/newsletter/paraguay-el-eden-de-los-conservadores-brasilenos">conservative influencers</a>, particularly from Brazil, who contrasted Paraguay’s economic model with the purported mismanagement of left-wing governments elsewhere in the region. Indeed, under President Santiago Peña, Paraguay has been one of Latin America’s most enthusiastic allies of the Trump administration and its expansive regional vision.</p>

<p>But beneath the financial stability, Ueno stood at the precipice of a much deeper problem.  </p>

<figure class="align-center ">
            <img alt="Two men in suites embrace hands." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770645/original/file-20261108-64-kverpg.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770645/original/file-20261108-64-kverpg.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770645/original/file-20261108-64-kverpg.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770645/original/file-20261108-64-kverpg.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770645/original/file-20261108-64-kverpg.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=502&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770645/original/file-20261108-64-kverpg.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=502&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770645/original/file-20261108-64-kverpg.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=502&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px">
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Congress President Basilio Núñez places the presidential sash on Pedro Alliana as he takes office as Paraguay’s new president on Nov. 6, 2026.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/Paraguay%20Bank%20Failure/9417d2fbccf64896bf299deb1380de0e/photo">AP Photo/Jorge Saenz</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>The central bank finally acted after accounting adjustments left Ueno’s solvency ratio below half the legal minimum. But problems had surfaced earlier. That included a supervisory report <a href="https://www.abc.com.py/politica/2026/10/12/ueno-movio-us-146-millones-hacia-tres-empresas-vinculadas/">put out by the bank regulators in June 2026</a> that described roughly US$146 million in loans to three companies linked to Grupo Vázquez, Ueno’s controlling shareholder. Some companies had been transferred to group employees; supervisors questioned the collateral and ultimate use of the funds.</p>

<p>That these warning signs went unheeded raises a related question of why regulators didn’t have a better handle on the situation and were not better able to contain the exposure.</p>

<p>In any case, Ueno’s problems were exposed in dramatic fashion on Nov. 2, when the central bank <a href="https://www.bcp.gov.py/web/institucional/w/banco-central-inicia-el-procedimiento-de-resolucion-de-ueno-bank/">placed Ueno</a> into resolution, a process similar to bankruptcy but managed directly by Paraguay’s central bank. The lender, which says it has nearly 3 million customers – about half of the country’s population – halted transactions.</p>

<p>The crisis quickly ensnared the governing party. Peña, an economist by training who was elected president in 2023 and had close ties to the bank, resigned on Nov. 5. The Senate then <a href="https://www.ultimahora.com/por-la-condena-congreso-fulmina-a-santiago-pena-y-lo-destituye-como-presidente-de-paraguay">voted unanimously</a> to remove him from office, thereby stripping Peña of his parliamentary immunity. He was swiftly put under house arrest, charged with corruption and succeeded by his Vice President <a href="https://www.ultimahora.com/pedro-alliana-jura-como-presidente-tras-destitucion-de-santiago-pena">Pedro Alliana, who was sworn</a> in to serve until 2028.   </p>

<p>Meanwhile, the crisis has led to widespread protests, including outside Congress, with citizens accusing Peña and the ruling Colorado Party of “<a href="https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-11-06/banking-crisis-plunges-paraguay-into-political-disarray/107355316">stealing” their savings</a>.</p>

<h2>When the regulator knows the regulated</h2>

<p>Part of the story of Ueno is a tale of the closeness between political and financial elites in Paraguay. </p>

<p>Carlos Carvallo chaired Ueno’s predecessor bank before Peña appointed him Paraguay’s central bank president in 2023. Carvallo <a href="https://www.reuters.com/business/finance/paraguays-central-bank-chief-resigns-presidents-request-digital-lender-crisis-2026-11-03/">resigned on Nov. 3</a> and has since <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/06/world/americas/paraguay-president-removed-ueno.html">been charged</a> with the same corruption crimes as Peña. For its part, the Paraguayan central bank says Carvallo recused himself from any Ueno decisions. </p>

<p>Yet the potential conflicts of interest ran much deeper. Peña previously directed Banco Basa, linked to Colorado Party leader and former President Horacio Cartes, who retains considerable influence and <a href="https://www.cbc.ca/news/world/paraguay-ueno-bank-crisis-pena-resignation-9.7410656">was instrumental in helping push</a> Peña out of office. Finance Minister Carlos Fernández Valdovinos also served on Basa’s board. Local reporters had documented these <a href="https://elsurti.com/laprecisa/chequeo/2024/02/26/de-basa-y-ueno-a-cargos-publicos-estrategicos-que-manejan-la-economia-y-las-finanzas-del-pais/">revolving-door relationships</a> early in Peña’s term.</p>

<p>Peña reportedly held a <a href="https://www.abc.com.py/politica/2025/04/04/santi-aparece-como-socio-de-red-mimada-con-contratos-del-estado/">1.58% stake in Ueno Holding</a>, which shared its principal shareholder, Grupo Vázquez, with Ueno bank. His brother Francisco held shares in <a href="https://www.abc.com.py/politica/2025/04/06/hermano-de-santi-era-parte-de-offshore-de-banco-favorito-dei-ips/">Luxembourg-based U Holdings</a>, an indirect shareholder in the bank. <a href="https://www.abc.com.py/politica/2025/04/06/hermano-de-santi-era-parte-de-offshore-de-banco-favorito-dei-ips/">Another shareholder</a> was Juan Carlos López Moreira, Cartes’ former chief of staff. Both brothers exited in 2025.</p>

<p><a href="https://www.reuters.com/business/finance/paraguays-ex-president-pea-faces-prosecutors-after-impeachment-house-arrest-2026-11-07/">Peña has denied any wrongdoing</a>, while prosecutors are examining allegations concerning his former business interests and his administration’s financial supervision. </p>

<p>The inclusion of significant reserves of public funds made these connections especially consequential. Ueno held approximately <a href="https://www.reuters.com/business/finance/what-is-ueno-bank-how-did-it-trigger-paraguays-political-crisis-2026-11-05/">$850 million in public funds</a>, including <a href="https://www.abc.com.py/nacionales/2026/11/05/ueno-bank-ips-abrio-proceso-de-proteccion-de-sus-fondos-ante-el-bcp/">$355 million from the country’s social security system</a>, IPS, including health and retirement funds. It amounted to roughly 9% of IPS’s investment portfolio. </p>

<p>Under Peña-appointed chairman Jorge Brítez, IPS <a href="https://www.abc.com.py/politica/2026/07/08/cambios-clave-en-el-ips-coincidieron-con-la-catarata-de-fondos-para-ueno-bank/">relaxed eligibility requirements for bank deposits</a> in 2023 and removed a capital-based exposure limit in 2024. Over the same period, its deposits at Ueno rose sharply. Grupo Vázquez’s technology firm ITTI won at least <a href="https://www.abc.com.py/economia/2025/03/12/contratos-de-itti-con-el-estado-se-triplicaron-durante-gobierno-de-pena-de-pequenas-facturaciones-paso-a-conseguir-g-17500-millones/">$2.3 million</a> in state contracts after Peña took office, versus $675,000 before. ITTI attributed the increase to business expansion and denied a conflict of interest.</p>

<p>Together these ties and regulatory changes raise important questions about <a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/3003160">regulatory capture</a> and other potential conflicts of interest.</p>

<h2>What the growth figures leave out</h2>

<p>Paraguay’s economic gains are real. In August, the <a href="https://www.imf.org/en/news/articles/2026/08/28/pr26280-paraguay-imf-executive-board-concludes-2026-article-iv-consultation">International Monetary Fund projected 4.4%</a> growth in 2026 following 6.6% in 2025. Moody’s granted the country’s debt <a href="https://ratings.moodys.com/ratings-news/425642">investment-grade status</a> in 2024, and S&amp;P <a href="https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2025-12-17/s-p-lifts-paraguay-rating-to-investment-grade-joining-moody-s">followed in</a> 2025. Hydroelectric power exports, agriculture and new infrastructure continue to underpin the economy.</p>

<figure class="align-center ">
            <img alt="People throw cards in a burning pile." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770646/original/file-20261108-64-g6p3bv.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770646/original/file-20261108-64-g6p3bv.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770646/original/file-20261108-64-g6p3bv.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770646/original/file-20261108-64-g6p3bv.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770646/original/file-20261108-64-g6p3bv.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=502&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770646/original/file-20261108-64-g6p3bv.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=502&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770646/original/file-20261108-64-g6p3bv.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=502&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px">
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Demonstrators burn Ueno bank cards during a protest after Paraguay’s central bank took over the bank amid a solvency crisis on Nov. 5, 2026.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/Paraguay%20Bank%20Failure/5584ddd878c24e088261f4f7b95d0cbc/photo">AP Photo/Jorge Saenz</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Washington is also drawing Paraguay more firmly into its regional economic strategy. On Oct. 23, the country became the <a href="https://www.mre.gov.py/paraguay-se-suma-a-la-declaracion-de-la-pax-silica/">26th signatory to the Pax Silica Declaration</a>, an initiative involving critical minerals, hydropower and advanced computing infrastructure. While the announcement did not specify financing commitments, it  shows how Paraguay’s resources and perceived political predictability are being positioned as strategic assets.</p>

<p>But growth figures and credit ratings say little about who shapes financial oversight or bears the costs of banking failures. Paraguay’s <a href="https://doi.org/10.1086/695715">legacies of political patronage</a> make it necessary to examine <a href="https://www.abc.com.py/politica/2026/07/13/exsocios-de-pena-crecieron-en-paralelo-a-fondos-publicos/">political and corporate connections</a> and changes to <a href="https://elsurti.com/laprecisa/chequeo/2024/02/26/de-basa-y-ueno-a-cargos-publicos-estrategicos-que-manejan-la-economia-y-las-finanzas-del-pais/">public-fund investment rules</a>.</p>

<h2>The social toll and the Colorado question</h2>

<p>Paraguay has been here before. Between 1995 and 1998, <a href="https://www.elibrary.imf.org/display/book/9781589064201/ch002.xml">13 banks and 35 financial firms closed</a>, with direct costs estimated by the IMF at 10% to 13% of the country’s GDP. This preceded a smaller <a href="https://www.hoy.com.py/nacionales/peirano-en-paraguay-la-quiebra-del-banco-aleman-y-otros-grandes-desfalcos-en-sudamerica">bank crisis</a> in the early 2000s. Both ordeals <a href="https://www.elibrary.imf.org/view/journals/087/2009/004/article-A001-en.xml">exposed weak supervision</a> and <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jfs.2013.07.005">connected lending</a>. </p>

<p><iframe id="wBEvt" class="tc-infographic-datawrapper" src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/wBEvt/6/" height="400px" width="100%" style="border: 0;" scrolling="no" frameborder="0" title="Table of different banking crises"></iframe></p>

<p>Paraguay’s deposit guarantee, which <a href="https://www.latintimes.com/paraguay-ueno-bank-collapse-president-resigns-600947">covers balances up to about $38,000</a>, is meant to limit depositor losses, and the Paraguayan Central Bank insists that <a href="https://www.latintimes.com/paraguay-ueno-bank-resolution-political-crisis-600886">failure is isolated</a> in the latest case. Yet account transfers have already <a href="https://www.usnews.com/news/world/articles/2026-11-05/explainer-what-is-ueno-bank-and-how-did-it-trigger-paraguays-political-crisis">strained the system</a>, producing outages at several banking institutions. </p>

<p>Yet for most Paraguayans, the crisis was experienced not through technical financial or macroeconomic indicators but at the stark level of seeing from their phones that they couldn’t access their money. Wages, pensions and savings <a href="https://www.latintimes.com/paraguay-ueno-bank-collapse-president-resigns-600947">froze simultaneously</a>. Young Ueno employees <a href="https://www.npr.org/2026/11/05/nx-s1-6030842/paraguay-president-impeached-bank-collapse">burned their company cards</a> outside the Labor Ministry, demanding unpaid wages. </p>

<p>Riot police used <a href="https://www.ibtimes.co.uk/paraguay-president-resigns-ueno-bank-crisis-1830483">pepper spray and rubber bullets</a> against depositors marching on Congress. For small businesses that banked and paid staff through Ueno, the real economy stopped. </p>

<p>This widespread anger challenges the ruling party’s claims to the economic vision they cite as the engine for future growth. Whether it leads to institutional change or a reshuffle within the Colorado Party remains an open question. The test is how Paraguayan legislators and regulators will move forward and whether they separate banking supervision and public deposits from partisan and business networks. </p>

<p>In any case, the myth of the “Dubai of South America” has come under serious scrutiny. While the protests were noteworthy, the Colorado Party has for now managed to resolve its own internal crisis by quickly sacrificing key political elites, including the president.</p>

<p><em>Marco Castillo Ph.D., Paraguayan sociologist, recent graduate and former director of research at the Center for Latin American, Latino and Caribbean Studies at Graduate Center CUNY, and Sheyla Rios Galeano, a Ph.D. Student in human dimensions of natural resources, Colorado State University, contributed to this article.</em></p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/296112/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

body: Protesters on Nov. 5 burn a effigy depicting now ex-President Santiago Pena outside Congress in Asuncion, Paraguay, days after the beginning of a banking crisis to which he was linked
AP Photo/Jorge Saenz It started on Nov. 3, 2026, when millions of Paraguayans trying to access the Ueno banking app found they could no longer get their money
In a matter of days, the financial situation escalated into political crisis, in which the country’s president was ousted, placed under house arrest and charged with several corruption-related crimes
The political and financial crisis exposes a central contradiction in Paraguay’s recent economic development
Ueno, a bank celebrated for expanding financial access to ordinary Paraguayans, grew through unusually close relationships with political elites and public institutions
And while the Ueno crisis came as a shock, there were clear warning signs

As scholars with expertise in various aspects of Paraguay’s contemporary political , economic and environment development , we believe the collapse raises troubling questions about who benefits from financial modernization, who controls it and who bears the risks when it fails

The political relationships through which financial institutions grow, regulators exercise authority and public resources are entrusted to private companies are crucial national concerns, especially in a country that has presented itself internationally as a model of economic stability
A bank that grew faster than scrutiny Founded as a digital lender in 2021, Ueno attracted customers with mobile banking and cash-back offers
Its expansion brought useful services to people underserved by conventional banks, including rural customers
Ueno also expanded the credit card market to low-income customers , an unprecedented move compared to previously restricted banking practices
As Ueno expanded, Paraguay increasingly attracted investors drawn by its low taxes, economic stability and business-friendly policies

Promoted by some as a “ Dubai of South America ,” the country also became a magnet for conservative influencers , particularly from Brazil, who contrasted Paraguay’s economic model with the purported mismanagement of left-wing governments elsewhere in the region
Indeed, under President Santiago Peña, Paraguay has been one of Latin America’s most enthusiastic allies of the Trump administration and its expansive regional vision
But beneath the financial stability, Ueno stood at the precipice of a much deeper problem
Congress President Basilio Núñez places the presidential sash on Pedro Alliana as he takes office as Paraguay’s new president on Nov. 6, 2026
AP Photo/Jorge Saenz The central bank finally acted after accounting adjustments left Ueno’s solvency ratio below half the legal minimum

That included a supervisory report put out by the bank regulators in June 2026 that described roughly US$146 million in loans to three companies linked to Grupo Vázquez, Ueno’s controlling shareholder
Some companies had been transferred to group employees; supervisors questioned the collateral and ultimate use of the funds
That these warning signs went unheeded raises a related question of why regulators didn’t have a better handle on the situation and were not better able to contain the exposure

In any case, Ueno’s problems were exposed in dramatic fashion on Nov. 2, when the central bank placed Ueno into resolution, a process similar to bankruptcy but managed directly by Paraguay’s central bank
The lender, which says it has nearly 3 million customers – about half of the country’s population – halted transactions
The crisis quickly ensnared the governing party
Peña, an economist by training who was elected president in 2023 and had close ties to the bank, resigned on Nov. 5
The Senate then voted unanimously to remove him from office, thereby stripping Peña of his parliamentary immunity
He was swiftly put under house arrest, charged with corruption and succeeded by his Vice President Pedro Alliana, who was sworn in to serve until 2028
Meanwhile, the crisis has led to widespread protests, including outside Congress, with citizens accusing Peña and the ruling Colorado Party of “ stealing” their savings
When the regulator knows the regulated Part of the story of Ueno is a tale of the closeness between political and financial elites in Paraguay
Carlos Carvallo chaired Ueno’s predecessor bank before Peña appointed him Paraguay’s central bank president in 2023
Carvallo resigned on Nov. 3 and has since been charged with the same corruption crimes as Peña
For its part, the Paraguayan central bank says Carvallo recused himself from any Ueno decisions
Yet the potential conflicts of interest ran much deeper
Peña previously directed Banco Basa, linked to Colorado Party leader and former President Horacio Cartes, who retains considerable influence and was instrumental in helping push Peña out of office
Finance Minister Carlos Fernández Valdovinos also served on Basa’s board
Local reporters had documented these revolving-door relationships early in Peña’s term
Peña reportedly held a 1.58% stake in Ueno Holding , which shared its principal shareholder, Grupo Vázquez, with Ueno bank
His brother Francisco held shares in Luxembourg-based U Holdings , an indirect shareholder in the bank
Another shareholder was Juan Carlos López Moreira, Cartes’ former chief of staff
Peña has denied any wrongdoing , while prosecutors are examining allegations concerning his former business interests and his administration’s financial supervision
The inclusion of significant reserves of public funds made these connections especially consequential

<title>5 ways countries stymie climate negotiations without actually saying ‘no’</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770593/original/file-20261106-64-rq0rx8.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=552%2C0%2C4417%2C2945&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Advisers for COP30 President Andre Correa do Lago, center, talk after a Colombia delegate&#39;s request to speak was overlooked at the U.N. summit in 2025.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/president-andre-correa-do-lago-gestures-next-to-his-news-photo/2247364584?phrase=colombia%20COP30&amp;adppopup=true">Pablo Porciuncula/AFP via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Nearly every country in the world has <a href="https://treaties.un.org/Pages/ViewDetails.aspx?src=TREATY&amp;mtdsg_no=XXVII-7-d&amp;chapter=27&amp;clang=_en">acknowledged that climate change is a serious problem</a>. It’s hard to ignore, as <a href="https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/syr/downloads/report/IPCC_AR6_SYR_SPM.pdf">billions of people suffer</a> through increasingly destructive storms and <a href="https://wmo.int/media/news/state-of-climate-2026-gives-new-meaning-phrase-charts">extreme heat</a>.</p>

<p>In response, most governments have promised repeatedly to cut greenhouse gas emissions that are <a href="https://www.csiro.au/en/research/environmental-impacts/climate-change/climate-change-qa/how-do-greenhouse-gases-warm-the-planet">driving global temperatures higher</a>. Yet <a href="https://www.reuters.com/sustainability/cop/30-years-climate-talks-progress-pitfalls-planet-peril-2025-11-06/">those emissions are still hitting record levels</a>, and global negotiations over how to slow climate change <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2025/nov/15/cop30-was-meant-to-be-a-turning-point-so-why-do-some-say-climate-summit-broken">routinely end with weak promises</a>.</p>

<p>There’s a reason: All it takes to water down a deal during these negotiations – the 2026 U.N. climate conference started Nov. 9 – are a few voices obstructing progress, often without ever saying “no,” and all the while maintaining the appearance of being a climate leader.</p>



<p><iframe id="immef" class="tc-infographic-datawrapper" src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/immef/4/" height="400px" width="100%" style="border: 0;" scrolling="no" frameborder="0" title="Global temperatures rising"></iframe></p>

<p>As a professor of <a href="https://dornsife.online.usc.edu/sm/faculty/shannon-gibson/">environmental studies and international relations</a> at the University of Southern California, I’ve attended and observed international climate negotiations for over a decade. <a href="https://www.gcjlab.com/">My research lab</a> investigates climate justice concerns and the forces that obstruct progress at the global U.N. climate talks.</p>

<p>As world leaders and their negotiators meet for the <a href="https://cop.sifiratikvakfi.org/en/">latest climate talks, COP31</a>, in Antalya, Turkey, Nov. 9-20, you can also pick out who is obstructing progress. Here are five tactics <a href="https://cssn.org/cssn-primer-climate-obstruction-in-the-unfccc/">among many</a> that powerful people at these conferences use to delay, weaken or redirect meaningful action while still appearing committed to addressing climate change:</p>

<h2>1. Say we can’t afford it</h2>

<p>“We don’t have the money” is a familiar refrain at U.N. climate negotiations.</p>

<p>At <a href="https://theconversation.com/un-climate-negotiations-end-on-shaky-geopolitical-ground-but-i-see-reasons-for-hope-243006">COP29</a> in Baku, Azerbaijan, in 2024, wealthy countries pointed to tight budgets, pandemic debt and rising inflation as reasons they could not meet the <a href="https://www.reuters.com/sustainability/sustainable-finance-reporting/wealthy-countries-back-raising-cop29-climate-deal-300-billion-sources-say-2024-11-23/">US$1.3 trillion in assistance that developing countries were demanding</a>. They instead offered $300 billion annually by 2035 as a finance target.</p>

<p>Poorer countries that did little to cause climate change want longtime fossil fuel users to pay for the damage emissions have caused. The COP29 agreement itself <a href="https://www.dawn.com/news/amp/1874623">estimated that developing countries’ climate needed</a> $5.1 trillion to $6.8 trillion in total through 2030.</p>

<p>In reality, affordability is really about priorities.</p>

<p>For example, the <a href="https://www.iisd.org/articles/press-release/governments-five-times-more-public-money-fossil-fuels-than-renewables">International Institute for Sustainable Development found</a> that governments around the world provided more than $1.2 trillion in public financial support for fossil fuels in 2024, about five times the $254 billion they provided for clean energy.</p>

<p><iframe id="yVr0n" class="tc-infographic-datawrapper" src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/yVr0n/1/" height="400px" width="100%" style="border: 0;" scrolling="no" frameborder="0" title="How much the U.S. gave to the Green Climate Fund vs. funding other countries to buy U.S. weapons"></iframe></p>

<p>Military budgets tell a similar story. Over the decade from 2014 to 2024, the U.S. contributed $2 billion to the Green Climate Fund, meant to support poorer countries as they adapt to climate change, <a href="https://www.nationalpriorities.org/analysis/2024/weapons-warming-world-us-contributions-green-climate-fund-vs-foreign-military-fi/">while Congress simultaneously approved at least $79 billion</a> to help foreign countries by U.S. military weapons. <a href="https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-59877-x">Recent research</a> points out that rising military spending makes climate goals even harder to reach because so much military activity runs on fossil fuels.</p>

<p>The money exists. The question is where governments choose to spend it.</p>

<h2>2. Promise to fix it later</h2>

<p>Another tactic is claiming that technological innovations will clean things up eventually, so <a href="https://doi.org/10.1088/1748-9326/ac0749">drastic emissions cuts can wait</a> or even be avoided. </p>

<p>This technological optimism has deep roots. In 2004, Princeton scholars Steve Pacala and Robert Socolow proposed the “<a href="https://acee.princeton.edu/wp-content/uploads/2018/06/Pacala-2004-Stabilization-Wedges-Solving-the-Climate-Problem-for-the-Next-50-Years-with-Current-Technologies.pdf">stabilization wedge</a>” approach to addressing climate change. It slices future emissions growth into 15 strategy wedges, each representing a way to cut 1 billion tons of carbon dioxide. Selecting from that menu, government could piece together a suitable emissions reduction strategy.</p>

<figure class="align-right zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770429/original/file-20261105-64-ylo7jl.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A cross-section of ground showing power plants and an oil rig and pipes going deep into the ground" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770429/original/file-20261105-64-ylo7jl.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=237&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770429/original/file-20261105-64-ylo7jl.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=710&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770429/original/file-20261105-64-ylo7jl.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=710&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770429/original/file-20261105-64-ylo7jl.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=710&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770429/original/file-20261105-64-ylo7jl.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=892&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770429/original/file-20261105-64-ylo7jl.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=892&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770429/original/file-20261105-64-ylo7jl.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=892&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Carbon capture and storage allows fossil fuel operations to continue by pumping their emissions underground.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:CBO-how-carbon-capture-works.png">Congressional Budget Office</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Renewable energy solutions such as solar and wind were proposed as wedges, but so were carbon capture and storage technologies – which would allow the burning of fossil fuels to continue.</p>

<p>Scientists, <a href="https://www.nationalgeographic.com/science/article/110517-global-warming-scientist-concern">including one of the original authors</a>, have claimed that the wedges approach makes a difficult problem look deceptively simple to solve. Recent reporting by ProPublica tracked money behind the wedges project back <a href="https://www.propublica.org/article/wedges-climate-research-bp-fossil-fuel-princeton">to the fossil fuel giant BP</a>.</p>

<p>Yet the same <a href="https://unfccc.int/sites/default/files/resource/cma5_auv_4_gst.pdf">logic is now present in agreements</a> emerging from recent climate talks. </p>

<h2>3. Water down the promise</h2>

<p>Another tactic is to agree to something, then water it down over time until it is no longer binding.</p>

<p>At <a href="https://theconversation.com/cop26-left-the-world-with-a-climate-to-do-list-here-are-5-things-to-watch-for-in-2022-172024">COP26</a> in Glasgow, Scotland, in 2022, early drafts of the agreement called for the “phasing out” of fossil fuels. It would have been a true milestone, as it was the first time the words “fossil fuels” had appeared in a climate agreement.</p>

<p>However, after a late push led by India, backed by China, South Africa and others, <a href="https://eandt.theiet.org/2021/11/12/cop26-cop-out-coal-fossil-fuel-phaseout-diluted">the final text was changed to “phasedown” of “unabated” coal power instead</a>. Additionally, the pact said nothing of oil and gas, the fuels that wealthier countries depend on most.</p>

<p><iframe id="tc-infographic-1535" class="tc-infographic" height="400px" src="https://cdn.theconversation.com/infographics/1535/f565cc63026e8a0396f5b780535497e4e36599de/site/index.html" width="100%" style="border: none" frameborder="0" title="COP31 glossary dropdown"></iframe></p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">

<p>The first fossil fuel language in a U.N. climate pact came out diluted. Four years later, at COP30, <a href="https://www.iisd.org/articles/insight/cop-30-outcome-what-it-means-and-whats-next">88 countries backed a roadmap</a> to move the world away from using fossil fuels, but the final decision left it out.</p>

<h2>4. Make promises, then fail to deliver</h2>

<p>Countries are really good at making pledges to help, but not so much at providing the funding.</p>

<p>In 2009, wealthy countries promised developing countries $100 billion annually to help them address climate risks. They <a href="https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-021-02846-3">missed that target for over a decade</a>. Even when they did claim to hit the target, they <a href="https://theconversation.com/how-climate-finance-to-help-poor-countries-became-a-global-shell-game-donors-have-counted-fossil-fuel-projects-airports-and-even-ice-cream-shops-268764">relied largely on dubious accounting</a>, with donors counting fossil fuel projects, airports and even ice cream shops as climate aid.</p>

<p>The <a href="https://theconversation.com/cop27s-loss-and-damage-fund-for-developing-countries-could-be-a-breakthrough-or-another-empty-climate-promise-194992">Loss and Damage Fund</a> created at <a href="https://theconversation.com/after-cop27-all-signs-point-to-world-blowing-past-the-1-5-degrees-global-warming-limit-heres-what-we-can-still-do-about-it-195080">COP27</a> in 2021 to help countries manage disaster damage shows a similar pattern. Only <a href="https://www.carbonbrief.org/analysis-nepals-20m-loss-and-damage-claim-only-covers-0-7-of-flood-costs">about half of the roughly $822 million pledged had been paid in</a> five years later, and the fund has not paid out a single dollar to a country hit by a disaster.</p>

<p><iframe id="yaEV3" class="tc-infographic-datawrapper" src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/yaEV3/1/" height="400px" width="100%" style="border: 0;" scrolling="no" frameborder="0" title="Map of countries that have requested money from the Loss and Damage Fund"></iframe></p>

<p><a href="https://progressive.org/latest/nepal-isnt-asking-for-charity-its-calling-in-a-debt-gibson-20261020/">Nepal has emerged as a critical test</a> of the fund’s integrity. After a glacier collapse triggered a sudden flood that killed more than 1,400 people in Nepal in August 2026, the government estimated the country had suffered <a href="https://www.reuters.com/business/environment/nepal-get-20-million-climate-fund-after-deadly-august-flood-2026-10-23/">$2.7 billion in damage</a>. Nepal requested $20 million, and, in a first, the fund’s board <a href="https://www.frld.org/sites/default/files/FRLD_Press_Release_Nepal_22Oct2026-2.pdf">agreed in October to “provisionally set aside</a>” $21.6 million, but that’s only the beginning of the paperwork.</p>

<h2>5. Make decisions without everyone at the table</h2>

<p>Decisions at the U.N. climate conference are taken by consensus, meaning they’re considered adopted when no country formally objects. This act is marked by the banging of a gavel.</p>

<p>At <a href="https://theconversation.com/why-the-cop28-climate-summit-mattered-and-what-to-watch-for-in-2024-220142">COP28</a> in Dubai, the conference president “gaveled through” a key decision before representatives of the Alliance of Small Island States had reached the room, meaning they had no chance to object. The lead negotiator for the islands’ group <a href="https://aosis.org/cop28-closing-plenary-aosis-statement-on-gst-decision/">told the meeting</a> that they would have objected, as they considered it too weak to keep warming to the agreed limit of 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 Fahrenheit) within reach.</p>

<p>In 2025, at <a href="https://theconversation.com/the-battle-over-a-global-energy-transition-is-on-between-petro-states-and-electro-states-heres-what-to-watch-for-in-2026-272205">COP30</a> in Belém, Brazil, a similar scene played out. </p>

<p>After swiftly gaveling through many decisions, the conference president failed to recognize Colombia’s request to speak until after the gavel had fallen. <a href="https://www.cbc.ca/news/world/cop30-deal-fossil-fuels-climate-change-crisis-9.6989208">Colombia objected that the text</a> of the formal decision failed to discuss a transition away from fossil fuels. The COP president <a href="https://www.theenergymix.com/breaking-empty-deal-at-cop30-as-petrostates-block-progress-on-fossil-fuel-phaseout/">later apologized</a> but said the decision could not be reopened.</p>

<h2>What to watch for at COP31</h2>

<p>At COP31, my team and I will be watching for decisions about financial support, whether talk of technology crowds out reducing fossil fuel use, and who gets a voice. </p>

<p>Much of what matters at these conferences happens out of the spotlight. <a href="https://unfccc.int/cop31/schedule">Plenary sessions</a>, where decisions are formally adopted, are the part most people see. But the wording of those decisions is usually worked out in smaller rooms and closed-door huddles among a handful of delegations. Small delegations can’t staff every room, and some rooms are closed to observers. </p>

<p>My team will be <a href="http://www.gcjlab.com/">tracking what happens</a>, whose proposals survive, and what quietly drops out between drafts of the agreement text. We’ll also be paying attention to who, quietly or not, says “no.” </p>

Pablo Porciuncula/AFP via Getty Images Nearly every country in the world has acknowledged that climate change is a serious problem
It’s hard to ignore, as billions of people suffer through increasingly destructive storms and extreme heat
In response, most governments have promised repeatedly to cut greenhouse gas emissions that are driving global temperatures higher
Yet those emissions are still hitting record levels , and global negotiations over how to slow climate change routinely end with weak promises

There’s a reason: All it takes to water down a deal during these negotiations – the 2026 U.N. climate conference started Nov. 9 – are a few voices obstructing progress, often without ever saying “no,” and all the while maintaining the appearance of being a climate leader
As a professor of environmental studies and international relations at the University of Southern California, I’ve attended and observed international climate negotiations for over a decade
My research lab investigates climate justice concerns and the forces that obstruct progress at the global U.N. climate talks
As world leaders and their negotiators meet for the latest climate talks, COP31 , in Antalya, Turkey, Nov. 9-20, you can also pick out who is obstructing progress
Here are five tactics among many that powerful people at these conferences use to delay, weaken or redirect meaningful action while still appearing committed to addressing climate change: 1
Say we can’t afford it “We don’t have the money” is a familiar refrain at U.N. climate negotiations

At COP29 in Baku, Azerbaijan, in 2024, wealthy countries pointed to tight budgets, pandemic debt and rising inflation as reasons they could not meet the US$1.3 trillion in assistance that developing countries were demanding
They instead offered $300 billion annually by 2035 as a finance target
Poorer countries that did little to cause climate change want longtime fossil fuel users to pay for the damage emissions have caused
The COP29 agreement itself estimated that developing countries’ climate needed $5.1 trillion to $6.8 trillion in total through 2030
In reality, affordability is really about priorities

For example, the International Institute for Sustainable Development found that governments around the world provided more than $1.2 trillion in public financial support for fossil fuels in 2024, about five times the $254 billion they provided for clean energy

Over the decade from 2014 to 2024, the U.S. contributed $2 billion to the Green Climate Fund, meant to support poorer countries as they adapt to climate change, while Congress simultaneously approved at least $79 billion to help foreign countries by U.S. military weapons
Recent research points out that rising military spending makes climate goals even harder to reach because so much military activity runs on fossil fuels
The question is where governments choose to spend it. 2
Promise to fix it later Another tactic is claiming that technological innovations will clean things up eventually, so drastic emissions cuts can wait or even be avoided
This technological optimism has deep roots
In 2004, Princeton scholars Steve Pacala and Robert Socolow proposed the “ stabilization wedge ” approach to addressing climate change
It slices future emissions growth into 15 strategy wedges, each representing a way to cut 1 billion tons of carbon dioxide
Selecting from that menu, government could piece together a suitable emissions reduction strategy
Carbon capture and storage allows fossil fuel operations to continue by pumping their emissions underground

Congressional Budget Office Renewable energy solutions such as solar and wind were proposed as wedges, but so were carbon capture and storage technologies – which would allow the burning of fossil fuels to continue
Scientists, including one of the original authors , have claimed that the wedges approach makes a difficult problem look deceptively simple to solve
Recent reporting by ProPublica tracked money behind the wedges project back to the fossil fuel giant BP
Yet the same logic is now present in agreements emerging from recent climate talks. 3
Water down the promise Another tactic is to agree to something, then water it down over time until it is no longer binding
At COP26 in Glasgow, Scotland, in 2022, early drafts of the agreement called for the “phasing out” of fossil fuels
It would have been a true milestone, as it was the first time the words “fossil fuels” had appeared in a climate agreement
However, after a late push led by India, backed by China, South Africa and others, the final text was changed to “phasedown” of “unabated” coal power instead
Additionally, the pact said nothing of oil and gas, the fuels that wealthier countries depend on most

<title>How protection of public land shapes political strategies in the American West</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770330/original/file-20261105-64-8x5wc9.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C205%2C5000%2C3333&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Parts of the Grand Staircase National Monument were removed from federal protection under the Trump administration, opening the way for mining and drilling.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/in-an-aerial-view-cliff-risers-and-level-benches-make-up-news-photo/2302810699">David McNew/Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Public lands are intricately woven into the fabric of America. Years of data confirms that a majority of Americans, regardless of their political beliefs, want <a href="https://www.coloradocollege.edu/other/stateoftherockies/conservationinthewest/2026.html">public lands to remain in federal hands</a> – though not everyone agrees on how exactly those lands should be managed. And while it’s not clear that public lands were a crucial factor in the 2026 midterm election results, survey data suggests that it is an <a href="https://www.coloradocollege.edu/other/stateoftherockies/conservationinthewest/2026.html">important issue in deciding whom to vote for</a>.</p>

<p>Federal conservation efforts <a href="https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R42346">began in the late 1800s</a>, with <a href="https://www.nps.gov/yell/learn/historyculture/index.htm">Yellowstone becoming the first national park</a> in 1872. Today, 640 million acres, <a href="https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R42346">nearly 30% of the country’s land area</a>, are administered by the federal government for a wide range of purposes, including conservation, forestry, grazing and energy production. These lands are held in trust by the federal government for the American people.</p>

<p>In our <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=rjUNwuAAAAAJ&amp;hl=en&amp;oi=ao">studies of the politics</a> of <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=yN01N-YAAAAJ&amp;hl=en&amp;oi=ao">the American West</a>, where the vast majority of U.S. public lands are located, we are seeing efforts to make voters aware of candidates’ views on land protection and to use grassroots political tactics to influence management decisions.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770335/original/file-20261105-93-cmlw5l.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="People stand on a staircase holding signs promoting public land and wilderness." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770335/original/file-20261105-93-cmlw5l.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770335/original/file-20261105-93-cmlw5l.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770335/original/file-20261105-93-cmlw5l.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770335/original/file-20261105-93-cmlw5l.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770335/original/file-20261105-93-cmlw5l.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770335/original/file-20261105-93-cmlw5l.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770335/original/file-20261105-93-cmlw5l.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">In 2017, moves to privatize public land sparked major protests, including in the Montana State Capitol.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/people-gather-at-the-state-capital-for-a-rally-in-support-news-photo/640423450">William Campbell/Corbis via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Land transfers</h2>

<p>Protesting government efforts to turn turn public spaces into private property, or to allow development on public land, are key ways people show the value they place on public lands.</p>

<p>In 2017, at the start of Donald Trump’s first term as president, U.S. Rep. Jason Chaffetz, a Utah Republican, <a href="https://democrats-naturalresources.house.gov/media/in-the-news/facing-backlash-utah-rep-jason-chaffetz-withdraws-bill-to-transfer-federal-land-to-the-states">proposed that the federal government transfer land to individual states</a>. The states, underfunded and understaffed to manage the land themselves, would <a href="https://www.trcp.org/public-land-access/">likely have sold the land to private interests</a>. The response created the <a href="https://www.boulderstrategiesllc.com/work/keepitpublic">#KeepItPublic social media campaign</a> and mobilized conservation groups against the bill. Land Tawney, president of Backcountry Hunters and Anglers, said, “<a href="https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2017/feb/02/republican-selling-public-lands-bill-withdraw-jason-chaffetz">Once that bill was introduced, the hornet’s nest was kicked</a>.” Chaffetz pulled the bill and left Congress five months later. </p>

<p>And in 2025, after Trump returned to the White House, U.S. Sen. Mike Lee, a Utah Republican, proposed that Congress require the U.S. Bureau of Land Management and the U.S. Forest Service to <a href="https://coloradonewsline.com/2025/06/13/mike-lee-sell-public-land-western-states/">sell between 2.2 million to 3.3 million acres of public land</a> in 11 Western states. He said the land sale would help “<a href="https://www.energy.senate.gov/wp-content/uploads/media/doc/NEW25680.pdf">address local housing needs</a>.” </p>

<p>But conservation groups and other Western lawmakers, including fellow Republican U.S. Sen. Tim Sheehy and Republican U.S. Rep. Ryan Zinke, also of Montana, declared the proposal a “<a href="https://www.washingtonexaminer.com/opinion/3457150/conservative-case-for-public-lands-ryan-zinke/">threat to the Montana way of life</a>” and forced Lee to withdraw the proposal.</p>

<h2>Public land management</h2>

<p>There isn’t available evidence to suggest that voters choose members of Congress based solely on their views or action about the management of public lands.</p>

<p>But elected officials often swiftly distance themselves from or outright oppose efforts to modify or eliminate public land protections. That response signals they believe their land protection stances play a role in how the public views them.</p>

<p>For example, Trump administration efforts to <a href="https://www.grandcanyontrust.org/sites/default/files/resources/Utah-National-Monuments-Survey-December-2024.pdf">reduce Bears Ears National Monument</a> and to <a href="https://www.padilla.senate.gov/newsroom/press-releases/padilla-schiff-costa-huffman-lead-bipartisan-congressional-push-to-stop-proposed-yosemite-land-transfer-to-trump-donor/">swap a parcel in Yosemite National Park</a> with a private developer <a href="https://www.energy.senate.gov/press/dem/heinrich-joins-bipartisan-congressional-push-to-stop-proposed-yosemite-land-transfer-to-trump-donor/">met with opposition from both parties in Congress</a>.</p>

<p>However, that opposition is not always successful at preventing development or natural resource extraction on public lands. In March and April 2026, both houses of Congress passed a resolution <a href="https://apnews.com/article/mining-moratorium-boundary-waters-senate-vote-3e3f0827d52dd6d37f5e554b804ff27c">supporting mining near the Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness</a> in Minnesota, despite public outcry about the potential pollution of a vast wilderness.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770341/original/file-20261105-64-1g06jc.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Two people paddle a canoe across water toward a rocky tree-lined shore." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770341/original/file-20261105-64-1g06jc.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770341/original/file-20261105-64-1g06jc.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770341/original/file-20261105-64-1g06jc.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770341/original/file-20261105-64-1g06jc.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770341/original/file-20261105-64-1g06jc.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770341/original/file-20261105-64-1g06jc.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770341/original/file-20261105-64-1g06jc.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>

            </figcaption>

<h2>Public lands in election politics</h2>

<p>In 2026, two new groups emerged to call attention to threats to public lands. <a href="https://www.outdoorlife.com/conservation/public-land-scorecards-wyoming-politicians/">Protect Wyoming</a> and <a href="https://www.outdoorlife.com/conservation/idaho-pac-for-public-lands">PAC for Public Lands</a> in Idaho both formed <a href="https://www.protectwyoming.org/">specifically to compile</a> and publicize elected officials’ <a href="https://www.pacforpubliclands.org/">public lands voting records</a>, especially when those votes affect people’s rights to hunt, fish and enjoy the outdoors. </p>

<p>These groups may be able to tap into core land protection values <a href="https://www.coloradocollege.edu/other/stateoftherockies/conservationinthewest/2026.html">broadly shared by many voters across the political spectrum</a>. That could put more direct and consistent pressure on politicians to protect public lands.</p>

<h2>Political headwinds</h2>

<p>The Trump administration has moved to limit people from mobilizing in support of public lands.</p>

<p>For instance, Trump’s <a href="https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-actions/2025/01/declaring-a-national-energy-emergency/">Jan. 20, 2025, executive order</a> declaring a “<a href="https://theconversation.com/the-us-energy-market-has-its-troubles-though-it-may-not-be-a-national-emergency-249336">national energy emergency</a>” has led the Department of the Interior to accelerate its review of proposals for oil and gas drilling, production and refining, and mining, along with other energy-related natural resource development. </p>

<p>A process that used to take one to two years has been <a href="https://www.doi.gov/pressreleases/department-interior-implements-emergency-permitting-procedures-strengthen-domestic">reduced to no more than a month</a>. That provides less time for people to review documents, understand what they say and decide how they feel about the proposals. However, <a href="https://www.wpr.org/news/15-states-wisconsin-sue-trump-fast-track-oil-gas-projects">15 states are now suing the Trump administration</a>, saying that fast-tracking violates federal law and seeking court orders to restore the previous process.</p>

<p>And in January 2026, the White House <a href="https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/01/08/2026-00178/removal-of-national-environmental-policy-act-implementing-regulations">Council on Environmental Quality</a> revised the rules around public comments on proposed federal land management actions. Government agencies are required under the <a href="https://www.epa.gov/nepa/how-citizens-can-comment-and-participate-national-environmental-policy-act-process">National Environmental Policy Act</a> to give the public a chance to comment on rule changes. It is the primary way the public can raise objections, question the thoroughness of the options, or to provide other evidence to help inform policy. The council significantly shortened, or in some cases eliminated, the time period during which the public may submit comments – though that decision has also been challenged in court, saying the <a href="https://biologicaldiversity.org/programs/public_lands/pdfs/Dkt.-1-Original-Complaint.pdf">Administrative Procedure Act</a> requires the original amount of public comment.</p>

            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Retaining the public trust</h2>

<p>How the government handles data center development may shed further light on the political power of public lands. Back in July 2025, Trump issued an executive order seeking to “<a href="https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-actions/2025/07/accelerating-federal-permitting-of-data-center-infrastructure/">utilize federally owned land and resources</a> for the expeditious and orderly development of data centers.”</p>

<p>In fall 2026, media outlets and <a href="https://ourpubliclandsandwaters.substack.com/p/blm-approves-first-ever-ai-data-center">advocacy groups called attention</a> to efforts to <a href="https://westernpriorities.org/2026/10/is-the-trump-administration-illegally-authorizing-data-centers-on-public-land/">develop data centers on public lands</a>, including <a href="https://www.reuters.com/legal/litigation/least-17-data-center-campuses-proposed-us-public-lands-group-says-2026-10-20/">at least 17 computing campuses</a> in six states. </p>

<p>Nearly two-thirds of Americans oppose data centers being built in their communities. Some politicians have <a href="https://www.padilla.senate.gov/newsroom/press-releases/padilla-wyden-merkley-demand-answers-over-planned-development-of-data-centers-on-public-lands/">questioned the deals on federal land</a>. </p>

<p>These centers were on the minds of voters in the midterm elections, nowhere more than in the Nevada gubernatorial race, <a href="https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/live-results-nevada-governor-midterm-election">where the Democratic challenger won on a platform to oppose projects on federal land</a>. Voter discontent may not stop the Trump administration from moving forward, but it all but guarantees that data centers on public lands will be an issue in the <a href="https://www.npr.org/2026/10/29/nx-s1-6022096/who-benefits-when-massive-ai-data-centers-come-to-town">2028 general election</a>. The degree to which the opposition gains political momentum could be another indicator of how the American public will act to continue to demand that public lands remain in public hands.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/295334/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

Years of data confirms that a majority of Americans, regardless of their political beliefs, want public lands to remain in federal hands – though not everyone agrees on how exactly those lands should be managed
And while it’s not clear that public lands were a crucial factor in the 2026 midterm election results, survey data suggests that it is an important issue in deciding whom to vote for
Federal conservation efforts began in the late 1800s , with Yellowstone becoming the first national park in 1872

Today, 640 million acres, nearly 30% of the country’s land area , are administered by the federal government for a wide range of purposes, including conservation, forestry, grazing and energy production
These lands are held in trust by the federal government for the American people

In our studies of the politics of the American West , where the vast majority of U.S. public lands are located, we are seeing efforts to make voters aware of candidates’ views on land protection and to use grassroots political tactics to influence management decisions
In 2017, moves to privatize public land sparked major protests, including in the Montana State Capitol

William Campbell/Corbis via Getty Images Land transfers Protesting government efforts to turn turn public spaces into private property, or to allow development on public land, are key ways people show the value they place on public lands
In 2017, at the start of Donald Trump’s first term as president, U.S
Jason Chaffetz, a Utah Republican, proposed that the federal government transfer land to individual states
The states, underfunded and understaffed to manage the land themselves, would likely have sold the land to private interests
The response created the #KeepItPublic social media campaign and mobilized conservation groups against the bill
Land Tawney, president of Backcountry Hunters and Anglers, said, “ Once that bill was introduced, the hornet’s nest was kicked .” Chaffetz pulled the bill and left Congress five months later
