Forest Service to sell between 2.2 million to 3.3 million acres of public land in 11 Western states
He said the land sale would help “ address local housing needs .” But conservation groups and other Western lawmakers, including fellow Republican U.S
Ryan Zinke, also of Montana, declared the proposal a “ threat to the Montana way of life ” and forced Lee to withdraw the proposal
Public land management There isn’t available evidence to suggest that voters choose members of Congress based solely on their views or action about the management of public lands
But elected officials often swiftly distance themselves from or outright oppose efforts to modify or eliminate public land protections
That response signals they believe their land protection stances play a role in how the public views them

For example, Trump administration efforts to reduce Bears Ears National Monument and to swap a parcel in Yosemite National Park with a private developer met with opposition from both parties in Congress
However, that opposition is not always successful at preventing development or natural resource extraction on public lands

In March and April 2026, both houses of Congress passed a resolution supporting mining near the Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness in Minnesota, despite public outcry about the potential pollution of a vast wilderness
Protests in support of the Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness have not stopped a nearby mining proposal
Anthony Souffle/The Minnesota Star Tribune via Getty Images Public lands in election politics In 2026, two new groups emerged to call attention to threats to public lands

Protect Wyoming and PAC for Public Lands in Idaho both formed specifically to compile and publicize elected officials’ public lands voting records , especially when those votes affect people’s rights to hunt, fish and enjoy the outdoors
These groups may be able to tap into core land protection values broadly shared by many voters across the political spectrum
That could put more direct and consistent pressure on politicians to protect public lands

<title>Voters rejected data centers in dozens of communities, fueling the narrative that opposition to the AI infrastructure contributed to the 2026 blue wave</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770566/original/file-20261106-64-5d4w1n.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C1%2C7882%2C5254&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">A woman in New Port Richey, Fla., voices her opposition to the construction of AI data centers on July 18, 2026.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/woman-holds-signs-during-a-nationwide-protest-against-ai-news-photo/2286055243?phrase=data%20centers%20protest&amp;adppopup=true"> Thomas Simonetti/AFP via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Data centers were on the ballot, both directly and indirectly, in the 2026 midterm elections.</p>

<p>A total of <a href="https://ballotpedia.org/Data_center-related_ballot_measures,_2026">41 local ballot initiatives concerning data centers</a> in 10 states were up for a vote. All but one resulted in <a href="https://www.wsj.com/tech/ai/the-election-day-revolt-that-threatens-americas-ai-boom-03a53b52">measures to restrict or limit</a> their development.</p>

<p>The centers also may have played a role in several high-profile contests. In Ohio’s <a href="https://www.wosu.org/2026-08-17/ohios-u-s-senate-candidates-recalibrate-their-stances-on-data-centers">race for a U.S. Senate seat</a>, Democratic challenger Sherrod Brown hammered incumbent Jon Husted for his past support of data centers. <a href="https://abcnews.com/Politics/texas-democrats-data-centers-winning-issue/story?id=137684995">In Texas, Gina Hinojosa</a> made Republican Gov. Greg Abbott’s track record of supporting tax breaks for data centers a focal point of her winning campaign. Her victory marked a historic break with decades of Republican control in the state. As governor-elect, she immediately <a href="https://www.reuters.com/world/us/texas-governor-elect-says-state-will-have-laws-shield-citizens-data-centers-2026-11-06">reaffirmed her campaign pledge</a> to pursue legislation protecting Texans from data centers.</p>

<p>According to <a href="https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/2026-elections/exit-polls">NBC exit poll data</a>, 56% of voters felt that data centers were a major or even a crucial factor in influencing their congressional vote. For Black voters, the share was even higher, at 68%. </p>

<p>Data centers are <a href="https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/IF12899">key components in artificial intelligence infrastructure</a>, housing the computing resources used to train AI models. These <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2026/10/05/upshot/data-center-scale.html">massive facilities</a> guzzle energy and water and are very noisy. Many Americans argue that their costs, in terms of <a href="https://www.cnbc.com/2026/09/06/ai-data-centers-are-transforming-rural-land-markets-fueling-backlash.html?msockid=3ef240ac8bed6dd42f96579a8a5d6c9d">land use</a>, higher <a href="https://www.msn.com/en-us/news/other/americans-say-rising-utility-costs-are-straining-their-budgets-they-re-blaming-data-centers/ar-AA2fTqVb?ocid=BingNewsVerp">utility bills</a> and <a href="https://www.texastribune.org/2026/10/20/data-centers-texas-air-quality-report-pollution-health-risks/">environmental degradation</a>, outweigh the benefits.</p>

<p>I’m a <a href="https://www.grinnell.edu/user/trish">professor of political science</a> who studies political parties, electoral politics and technology. My forthcoming book, “Democratic Intelligence: Navigating Electoral Politics in an AI World,” examines how the adoption of this technology is reshaping established practices and power dynamics in campaigns. </p>

<p>Before the midterms, it had already appeared to be disrupting some partisan alignments. Following those historic elections, which have thoroughly shaken up America’s political geography, the widespread pushback against data centers is now part of the narrative explaining the dramatic results of the 2026 midterms. </p>

<h2>Disrupting political polarization</h2>

<p>In contrast to <a href="https://www.pewresearch.org/science/2026/05/28/americans-are-increasingly-pessimistic-about-avoiding-the-worst-effects-of-climate-change/">many other issues</a>, concern about data centers is relatively bipartisan. The Annenberg Public Policy Center asked Americans in mid-2026 whether they <a href="https://www.annenbergpublicpolicycenter.org/wp-content/uploads/AI_W38_Topline.pdf">support or oppose having data centers</a> in their communities. Opposition was stronger among Democrats, at 69%, than Republicans, at 54%, but it crossed party lines.</p>

<p>Local ballot measures restricting data centers also cut across traditional political alignments. Communities as disparate as deeply red Edgewater, Florida, and solidly blue Alhambra, California, voted to prohibit them. The margins for the restrictions were large, averaging 49 percentage points. </p>

<p>The one restrictive local measure that failed to pass was in <a href="https://www.business-standard.com/amp/world-news/us-midterms-only-one-town-out-of-dozens-voted-in-favor-of-data-centres-126110500119_1.html">Harwood, North Dakota</a>, population around 800. With a data center project already in progress, political and economic leaders prevailed in arguing that restrictions would cut into local revenue and stifle economic development more generally.</p>



<h2>Allies and adversaries</h2>

<p>Exit polls taken during the midterm elections also detected a degree of bipartisanship. Of the 56% of voters who said data centers <a href="https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/2026-elections/exit-polls">played a “major” or “crucial” role in their vote</a>, approximately two-thirds were Democrats and one-third Republicans. Exit polls, however, should be <a href="https://ballotpedia.org/Exit_polling">interpreted with care</a>, given their methodological limitations.</p>

<p>These responses hint at why the <a href="https://www.wired.com/story/the-results-are-in-voters-hate-data-centers/?_sp=c73d4ceb-72c9-4592-93e3-3f88045871f3.1793948422531.9d7e2aab-fdd0-4fd4-be05-bd938fd0a1a8">narrative</a> that opposition to data centers helped fuel the Democrats’ historic midterm victory emerged right away.</p>

<p>The seeds of this argument were in place before the election, picking up on unusual alliances that marked the data center opposition. In cities and counties, zoning fights are <a href="https://www.ap.org/news-highlights/elections/2026/in-a-divided-america-the-left-and-right-unite-to-oppose-artificial-intelligence-data-centers/">drawing a diverse kind of resistance</a>: environmentalists, voters reeling under high electricity costs, local-control advocates and farmers concerned that data centers eat up land. They unite in opposition to projects backed by powerful corporate interests.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770607/original/file-20261107-64-mia2u6.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A man stands outside speaking behind a William Lawrence campaign sign surrounded by people holding signs objecting to data centers." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770607/original/file-20261107-64-mia2u6.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770607/original/file-20261107-64-mia2u6.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770607/original/file-20261107-64-mia2u6.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770607/original/file-20261107-64-mia2u6.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770607/original/file-20261107-64-mia2u6.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770607/original/file-20261107-64-mia2u6.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770607/original/file-20261107-64-mia2u6.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">William Lawrence, a Democrat who flipped a red House seat in Michigan in the 2026 midterm elections, speaks on the campaign trail.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/Election%202026%20Michigan/8c3361c2fc634795933876e1b56fc4e6/photo">AP Photo/Paul Sancya</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Some of the bipartisanship around this issue has even seeped into Congress. Several weeks before Election Day, the House passed the <a href="https://www.politico.com/news/2026/09/16/house-passes-bill-data-center-power-costs-01076743">Ratepayer Protection Act</a> by a 417-3 vote. The bill would require states to consider adopting a policy that data centers pay for the upgrades necessary to meet their high electricity needs. The three nay House votes were from progressives who felt the bill’s measures, which would be voluntary, didn’t go far enough to protect consumers.</p>

<p>Similar concerns <a href="https://thehill.com/policy/energy-environment/6119834-senate-data-center-bill-ratepayer-protection-act/">killed the Senate version</a>, a reminder that even allies sometimes follow different strategic paths. Some proponents of tighter regulation will accept incremental progress, while others push for more sweeping change.</p>

<p><a href="https://www.brookings.edu/articles/how-the-2026-midterms-could-reshape-data-center-policy/">Brookings Institution scholars</a> anticipate that the newly elected Congress will take up the issue again, this time with a directive to states to establish mandatory, not voluntary, requirements.</p>

<h2>Politics as usual</h2>

<p>As the midterm elections approached, candidates up and down the ballot <a href="https://adimpact.com/blogs/2026-ad-messaging-snapshot-the-quiet-boom-in-data-center-ads">blanketed the airwaves</a> and digital platforms with <a href="https://campaignsandelections.com/industry-news/ai-data-centers-emerge-as-a-hot-topic-for-political-ads-in-2026/">ads against data centers</a>. <a href="https://truthsocial.com/@realDonaldTrump/posts/117190477440173795">President Donald Trump</a> pushed back, suggesting that data center opponents want their communities to be “backwards and poor.”</p>

<p><a href="https://apnews.com/article/ai-data-centers-trump-election-cd2cfd73e3d41e2baf65bf82702a589b">Some Republican candidates</a> walked a fine line between responding to voters’ concerns and not alienating the president.</p>

<p>It matters little whether the data center electoral narrative is accurate, and so far, the reported evidence is limited. We need to know where losing candidates stood on data centers, not just the winners. That voters considered data centers important says nothing about which direction they leaned. And despite a 98% success rate across the 41 local ballot measures, it’s hard to gauge how much resistance there is to the more than <a href="https://datacenterwatch.ai">600 proposed data centers</a> that are slated to be built.</p>

<p>What does matter is that many people apparently are accepting the narrative because that alone will affect politics and the economy. Consider <a href="https://x.com/elonmusk/status/2117862462976594112">Elon Musk’s post on Nov. 4 on X, his social media platform</a>: “Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now,” and the <a href="https://apnews.com/article/stocks-markets-ai-midterm-oil-trump-7ee9c212805aa5e70cf34d25aab7a36e">sell-off of data center-related stocks</a> the next day.</p>

<p>As the 2028 presidential primaries come into focus, I believe we should expect to see many Democratic and Republican hopefuls emphasizing their support for data center restrictions and bans as they throw their hats into the ring.</p>

excerpt: A woman in New Port Richey, Fla., voices her opposition to the construction of AI data centers on July 18, 2026
body: A woman in New Port Richey, Fla., voices her opposition to the construction of AI data centers on July 18, 2026
Thomas Simonetti/AFP via Getty Images Data centers were on the ballot, both directly and indirectly, in the 2026 midterm elections
A total of 41 local ballot initiatives concerning data centers in 10 states were up for a vote
All but one resulted in measures to restrict or limit their development
The centers also may have played a role in several high-profile contests
Senate seat , Democratic challenger Sherrod Brown hammered incumbent Jon Husted for his past support of data centers
In Texas, Gina Hinojosa made Republican Gov
Greg Abbott’s track record of supporting tax breaks for data centers a focal point of her winning campaign
Her victory marked a historic break with decades of Republican control in the state
As governor-elect, she immediately reaffirmed her campaign pledge to pursue legislation protecting Texans from data centers
According to NBC exit poll data , 56% of voters felt that data centers were a major or even a crucial factor in influencing their congressional vote
For Black voters, the share was even higher, at 68%
Data centers are key components in artificial intelligence infrastructure , housing the computing resources used to train AI models
These massive facilities guzzle energy and water and are very noisy
Many Americans argue that their costs, in terms of land use , higher utility bills and environmental degradation , outweigh the benefits
I’m a professor of political science who studies political parties, electoral politics and technology

My forthcoming book, “Democratic Intelligence: Navigating Electoral Politics in an AI World,” examines how the adoption of this technology is reshaping established practices and power dynamics in campaigns
Before the midterms, it had already appeared to be disrupting some partisan alignments

Following those historic elections, which have thoroughly shaken up America’s political geography, the widespread pushback against data centers is now part of the narrative explaining the dramatic results of the 2026 midterms
Data centers, like these near Social Circle, Ga., require enormous amounts of electricity
AP Photo/Mike Stewart Disrupting political polarization In contrast to many other issues , concern about data centers is relatively bipartisan
The Annenberg Public Policy Center asked Americans in mid-2026 whether they support or oppose having data centers in their communities
Opposition was stronger among Democrats, at 69%, than Republicans, at 54%, but it crossed party lines
Local ballot measures restricting data centers also cut across traditional political alignments
Communities as disparate as deeply red Edgewater, Florida, and solidly blue Alhambra, California, voted to prohibit them
The margins for the restrictions were large, averaging 49 percentage points
The one restrictive local measure that failed to pass was in Harwood, North Dakota , population around 800
With a data center project already in progress, political and economic leaders prevailed in arguing that restrictions would cut into local revenue and stifle economic development more generally
Allies and adversaries Exit polls taken during the midterm elections also detected a degree of bipartisanship
Of the 56% of voters who said data centers played a “major” or “crucial” role in their vote , approximately two-thirds were Democrats and one-third Republicans
Exit polls, however, should be interpreted with care , given their methodological limitations
These responses hint at why the narrative that opposition to data centers helped fuel the Democrats’ historic midterm victory emerged right away
The seeds of this argument were in place before the election, picking up on unusual alliances that marked the data center opposition

In cities and counties, zoning fights are drawing a diverse kind of resistance : environmentalists, voters reeling under high electricity costs, local-control advocates and farmers concerned that data centers eat up land
They unite in opposition to projects backed by powerful corporate interests
William Lawrence, a Democrat who flipped a red House seat in Michigan in the 2026 midterm elections, speaks on the campaign trail
AP Photo/Paul Sancya Some of the bipartisanship around this issue has even seeped into Congress
Several weeks before Election Day, the House passed the Ratepayer Protection Act by a 417-3 vote
The bill would require states to consider adopting a policy that data centers pay for the upgrades necessary to meet their high electricity needs
The three nay House votes were from progressives who felt the bill’s measures, which would be voluntary, didn’t go far enough to protect consumers

title: Christians are now getting freaked out by Trump
excerpt: In his first sit-down interview since the midterm elections, President Donald Trump speaks with Ross Douthat in the Roosevelt Room at the White House. | CBS New
body: In his first sit-down interview since the midterm elections, President Donald Trump speaks with Ross Douthat in the Roosevelt Room at the White House. | CBS News via Getty Images Every week, millions of Christians gather to worship and remember the tenets of the faith: belief in God, in Jesus Christ as his son and their savior, and in the Holy Spirit
Many utter the words of the Lord’s Prayer each week, and in doing so, ask that God forgive our sins, as we forgive those who trespass against us

These are the ABCs of the Christian faith — and they should theoretically be an easy answer to offer if, like President Donald Trump, you’re asked what might happen when you die, and what you might do when Judgment Day comes

And yet, when asked last week by Ross Douthat on 60 Minutes where Trump thinks he’ll go when he dies — and if he could forgive his political enemies if his salvation depended on it — Trump was brutally honest. “Well, I’m a religious person, so in theory I go to heaven,” the president said. “I hope so

I don’t want to go to hell.” Could he forgive opponents like former FBI Director James Comey and former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi? “Well, then I wouldn’t be real, would I? I mean, if I said to you, sure, the easy answer to that is ‘Oh, yes, I could forgive,’” Trump told Douthat. “The answer is no

I want to be honest, no.” Even if God asked it? “Before the judgment, no,” he said. “I do hate some of my enemies…I probably cannot do that, no, because I do hate some of my enemies and I always will.” “I'm a religious person, so in theory I go to heaven,” President Trump says, discussing what he thinks happens after death. “I don't want to go to hell.” https://t.co/8o5y8hcqtY pic.twitter.com/5LexpK2jEP — 60 Minutes (@60Minutes) November 9, 2026 The statements shook many Christians who watched clips or heard him say this on CBS

Perhaps the most interesting reaction has come from the religious right, from evangelicals, Catholics, and other Christians who have long sided with the president over the last decade of MAGA.  They’ve long defended him, seeing him and his movement as a vehicle to spread the Christian gospel and win policy victories, like banning abortion, restricting IVF, and fighting back against the rising tide of social progressivism

But in the wake of stunning losses for Republicans in last week’s midterm elections, when Trump’s grip on the GOP seems most tenuous, another crack seems to have emerged in his alliance with the Christian right

And that’s because his answers essentially removed the plausible deniability of the argument that many Christians have used to justify their votes for Trump: that though an “ imperfect vessel ,” he was still a Christian, had received the gospel, and wants to be saved
His close ally, the evangelical pastor Franklin Graham, explained the importance of the question (but did not directly address Trump’s forgiveness response) in a post on X: “Heaven has borders
Heaven has unique and very strict entrance requirements

To enter Heaven, the Bible tells us that you must acknowledge your sins, turn from them in repentance, and receive Jesus Christ by faith.” Trump’s response to the question about heaven, though, showed no understanding of these requirements. “Religion can’t save you — only a relationship with the Savior, Jesus Christ, can save you,” Graham continued. “Do you have that assurance?”  In unambiguous terms, Trump basically said he doesn’t

Why conservative Christians are actually divided over Trump this time That someone like Graham, one of the most widely respected American evangelical leaders, would weigh in at all this time shows how serious the concerns are among conservative Christians

In previous moments this year, when Trump has similarly tested the religious right , it was easier to dismiss blasphemy, in part because it was directed at Catholics like Pope Leo XIV and his bishops (with whom politically conservative Catholics tend to have disagreements) , or could be dismissed as a joke — as when he shared AI art of himself as Jesus Christ
After strong backlash from evangelicals over that meme, he backed down and deleted the post

This time, the criticism is coming from all over — from theological conservatives like the Eastern Orthodox Rod Dreher , from evangelicals and other Christians , from Catholics — and that’s because there are multiple problematic layers to his most recent polemic

For the longest time, it was easier for Trump allies to say that though he was an imperfect sinner , Trump could still be saved , could still do good for their movement , or argue that he was still a Christian

But that’s much harder to do when he is failing multiple tests — including the most important one for evangelicals: having and declaring a personal relationship and belief in Jesus Christ is kind of the main thing , the key to being able to call yourself a Christian and have hope of being saved at the hour of judgment
Being “religious” doesn’t get you to heaven; being saved by grace through faith in Christ does

Graham summed it quickly when describing what it means to “receive Jesus Christ by faith”: “That means, believe that Jesus Christ is God’s Son, that He paid the penalty for your sins by dying on a cross, was buried in a tomb, raised to life on the third day, and walked out of that tomb.” I watched @CBS @60Minutes tonight, and Ross Douthat interviewed President @realDonaldTrump
Toward the end of the interview, they talked about something far more important than politics

He asked the President, at 80 years of age and after surviving multiple assassination… — Franklin Graham (@Franklin_Graham) November 9, 2026 That Trump was unable to say this to Douthat throws a wrench in one of the common defenses of the authenticity of Trump’s faith

And to some evangelicals, the fact Trump wasn’t able to say this was revelatory: a sign that none of the ministers, priests, pastors, or faithful who work for him have been able to convert his heart or help him be born-again

The evangelical theologian Al Mohler, the president of the Southern Baptist Theological Seminary, put it this way on his podcast on Monday: “It’s also very clear that [Trump] certainly needs to hear the gospel.” He continued to say that he will be “praying for him, with a renewed sense of urgency, that he has an experience of grace that he comes to know the Lord Jesus Christ as savior, that he knows the forgiveness of sins.” It’s that second point about forgiveness that got Trump in trouble with more Christians — forgiving your enemies, and praying for them, is one of the core tenets of the Christian faith, and of gospel teachings
Dreher also referenced this part in his X post when he referred to “the pettiness and hatred in that man’s heart
He is literally a character in Dante’s Inferno

Despite being given so much in life, he hates his enemies more than he fears God.” Now, none of this is to say that Trump has fully lost the Christian right — most of the evidence points to evangelical Christians and a collection of other Protestant, Mormon, and other Christians still backing him and the GOP in polling and elections, albeit by smaller shares than before
But for the first time in the decade-long Trump era, his hold on this movement is precarious
After appearing to compromise on a range of priorities for them , he and the GOP have suffered a once-in-a-generation loss
Trump is now digging into a nihilist, “ post-Christian ” identity, in Dreher’s words, demonstrating he is unrepentant even in defeat
This all puts the religious right in uncharted waters
Years ago, Douthat himself pondered what American politics and society might look like if the right gave up on God
Now, in the wake of political devastation for the right, he has presented a new question: What might the religious right look like if it gave up on Trump?

title: Trump’s mixed messages on immigration
excerpt: Stephen Miller waits in the presidential limo as Donald Trump speaks to reporters in West Palm Beach, Florida, on November 6, 2026. | Samuel Corum/Getty Images
body: Stephen Miller waits in the presidential limo as Donald Trump speaks to reporters in West Palm Beach, Florida, on November 6, 2026. | Samuel Corum/Getty Images This story appeared in  The Logoff , a daily newsletter that helps you stay informed about the Trump administration without letting political news take over your life.  Subscribe here

Welcome to The Logoff: Is Donald Trump’s immigration agenda about to get even more draconian — or less?  What’s happening? As of Monday, immigration hardliner Stephen Miller — and if anything, “hardliner” undersells it — is Trump’s new chief of staff.  Miller, who was also a senior aide in Trump’s first term, is an ideologue and the force behind many of Trump’s harshest immigration policies, such as a 3,000-arrests-per-day quota for ICE officers; broadly speaking, his elevation forebodes an even darker and more aggressive final two years of Trump’s presidency

It’s also sharply in contrast with Trump’s recent comments on immigration in his first sit-down interview since his party’s midterms wipeout.  What did Trump say? In an interview with 60 Minutes ’s Ross Douthat that aired Sunday, Trump not only conceded that some of his immigration policies “might be too tough” and had hurt his party at the polls, but he floated the possibility that a bipartisan immigration deal could be “actually doable.”  “There’s a large part of the country that thinks that they should be allowed to stay if they’re good people working in a landscaping company or working in a hotel or doing something,” Trump told Douthat.  What’s the context? Trump has occasionally flirted with immigration legislation, including a first-term proposal pairing a citizenship deal for DACA recipients with border wall funding and legal immigration cuts that never went anywhere

More recently, in June 2025, he expressed similar concerns about the impact of immigration enforcement on hospitality and agriculture, but the change didn’t live out the week .  Will anything come of this? Anything’s possible, especially with powerful Democratic majorities incoming

But it hasn’t happened yet, and with Miller in the chief of staff’s office, it remains unlikely, to say the least. (Plus, some very loud parts of his own party absolutely hate the idea .) On Monday, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, the likely next speaker of the House, said  Miller “is a stone-cold racist. … I’ve got zero interest in working with that kind of individual.” And with that, it’s time to log off… Have you seen an “Ask me about metro” hat out in the wild recently? What about an ugly Christmas sweater with a train on it?  If so, you’re not alone: Public transit merch, The Atlantic reported , has been experiencing a boom lately. (I’m not immune to it: I have an Amtrak poster on my wall.) You can read all about the trend with a gift link here .  Have a great evening, and we’ll see you tomorrow!

title: Sex, spies, and microchips
excerpt: Jensen Huang, CEO of Nvidia, pictured at the Invest in Germany Summit on October 19, 2026 in Berlin. | Thomas Koehler/Photothek via Getty Images This story appe
body: Jensen Huang, CEO of Nvidia, pictured at the Invest in Germany Summit on October 19, 2026 in Berlin. | Thomas Koehler/Photothek via Getty Images This story appeared in Today, Explained, a daily newsletter that helps you understand the most compelling news and stories of the day
The movie version of Jensen Huang’s jaw-dropping affair basically writes itself
Cast BD Wong as 63-year-old Huang, the CEO of one of the world’s most valuable companies and a close friend of President Donald Trump

Kelly Hu can play Alice Huang, Jensen’s paramour and — even better — a purported agent of the Chinese government.  The role of Trump himself, who reportedly knew about Huang’s undercover girlfriend but on Sunday said Huang “probably has an excuse for it,” can be played by Alec Baldwin. (Or a flightless duck — your pick.) However you cast it, this whole sordid affair has “serialized Netflix drama” written all over it
But in all seriousness…the possibility that one of the world’s most powerful men was targeted by Chinese intelligence is a big deal on multiple scores
Nvidia has opened its own investigation into whether Huang was compromised, and congressional leaders have requested he brief them in a closed-door session

Nvidia supplies much of the computing power behind the AI boom, giving it enormous influence over the broader economy. “If they sneeze, everybody else catches a cold,” the writer and economic commentator Kyla Scanlon told Vox’s Today, Explained podcast last year
That makes this whole episode a little more weighty than your standard billionaire’s affair
Go a little deeper View Link Nvidia is the most valuable company on Earth — but in many households, it’s still not a household name

Huang and two other electrical engineers founded the now-$4.5-trillion company in 1993 with the fairly niche and nerdy goal of making high-powered chips that could render the 3D graphics for a new generation of video games.  Then, in 2006, the company released software tools that let programmers use its chips for other demanding computing tasks, like mining cryptocurrency and training AI models
When companies like OpenAI began developing tools like ChatGPT, they immediately turned to Nvidia.  That made the company a cornerstone of America’s AI buildout and a major economic force
In 2024, Nvidia alone accounted for more than a fifth of the S&P 500’s total return
And the rush to build out AI infrastructure has accounted for much of America’s recent economic growth , according to St
Nvidia’s influence extends to the White House, too , where Huang is a regular guest of Trump

The two became fast friends after having dinner together at Mar-a-Lago last year, and Huang has said Trump regularly calls him late at night to discuss topics like “protecting national security” and “creating more jobs.” But Huang’s ambitions have run up against one major obstacle: US restrictions on selling Nvidia’s most advanced chips to China
US officials worry that their enormous computing power could help Beijing develop weapons, strengthen its military, expand surveillance, and otherwise rival US military and technological dominance
That helps explain why China (allegedly) sicced a spy on Huang: They really want these chips

The New York Times reports that China’s top intelligence agency recruited Alice Huang both to learn more about America’s advanced chip industry and to potentially influence Nvidia’s push to lift export restrictions

Alice Huang, it should be noted, was a data center executive in her own right, and her company  has been investigated for purportedly helping to smuggle Nvidia chips into China.  All these investigations will hopefully, eventually, reveal whether their affair compromised anything beyond Huang’s marriage
They may also test how dependent Nvidia is on his leadership.  For now, Huang is staying on as CEO
But uncertainty over his future could unsettle investors and trigger wobbles in the wider market
That’s the problem with concentrating so much power in any one person or company: One person’s (very) personal business can somehow become everybody’s problem.  One link for later ➨ Get a hobby
But not just any hobby: something that’s intentionally imperfect, unproductive or unquantified
There’s a tendency in American culture to try to optimize or commodify our leisure , the writer Jenny Odell explains
But that undermines some of leisure’s biggest benefits — like cultivating a sense of joy, wonder, or learning
Before you go… Did you know… that Alexander Graham Bell reportedly wanted people to answer the phone with a cheerful “ahoy” ? Alas, Thomas Edison’s preferred greeting — “hello” — won out instead
Today’s trivia: Cleopatra was killed by what animal, according to several contemporaneous accounts? (You can find this and other brain puzzles in Vox’s daily crossword
Look for the answer in tomorrow’s edition.) Yesterday’s trivia: Last week we asked you for Ricky Martin’s biggest hit
That would be “ Livin’ La Vida Loca ,” the 1999 bop that’s widely credited with launching the Latin pop explosion of the late 1990s and early 2000s.

title: Can this progressive YIMBY fix one city’s ludicrous housing prices?
excerpt: Los Angeles Mayor-elect Nithya Raman at an election night party, November 3, 2026. | Sarah Reingewirtz/MediaNews Group/Los Angeles Daily News via Getty Images I
body: Los Angeles Mayor-elect Nithya Raman at an election night party, November 3, 2026. | Sarah Reingewirtz/MediaNews Group/Los Angeles Daily News via Getty Images It’s notoriously hard to govern Los Angeles, a city that gives its mayor less direct authority over the government than in a city like New York or Chicago

But even so, it’d be hard to do much worse than Karen Bass.  Elected mayor of LA in 2022, Bass campaigned on promises to solve the city’s homelessness and housing affordability crises (which are really part of the same underlying crisis )
She then spent her term undermining her own administration’s affordable housing policy and fighting the state of California’s efforts to compel cities to allow more housing production

She lost her bid for reelection this week to Nithya Raman, an LA City Council member, rising progressive star, and nationally prominent YIMBY.  Los Angeles has the highest ratio of home price to household income of any large city in America, and the second fewest homes per adult of any major city

It has a highly suburbanized and car-oriented fabric, like much of the rest of the country — all of which makes it a kind of proving ground for whether America’s sprawling cities can build their way out of their housing shortages.  Everyone in the city’s political leadership notionally agrees that LA needs to permit a lot more homes to meet demand — the only true way to make housing affordable — but not all of them have evidently had the policy discipline to follow through.  Raman may be different

She has gained a following in housing reform circles over the last few years with her brisk, direct-to-camera social videos explaining how LA’s housing shortage drives up rents and criticizing city policies that make it so difficult to build more homes (perhaps it’s no surprise that she has plenty of friends in Hollywood ). “There has been an overall lack of urgency in addressing housing supply in [Bass’s] administration,” Raman told me in an interview in July

How best to accommodate LA’s need for more housing, she said, is “a question that the city has actually turned away from.” Even given LA’s relatively weak mayoralty, Bass’s failures on housing were often a matter of political choice

As The Atlantic’s Marc Novicoff put it , “Bass seems to have gone out of her way to exercise as little power as possible.” Where she did go out of her way to wield her influence, it was often to stop denser housing from being built

Some of her bewildering housing policy choices while in office include:  Days into her term, Bass signed her first executive order, known as ED1, to fast-track housing developments where 100 percent of the apartments are affordable
Applications for these projects were to get approvals within 60 days instead of being dragged through excruciating permitting processes
It was a good idea — and it seemed to be working, quickly attracting developer applications to build thousands of affordable apartments
It was working so well, in fact, that a backlash from vocal NIMBYs followed

Less than six months after signing ED1, in June 2023, Bass weakened it to exclude projects in single-family neighborhoods — which make up three-quarters of LA’s residential land — from the fast-track approval process

Her administration even tried to apply that restriction retroactively to developments that had already applied to build in single-family areas under ED1, a breathtaking display of bureaucratic dysfunction; a judge later ruled that this violated California law
Bass has since added more restrictions to the ED1, and one observer has described it as “functionally gutted” for many developers

To be fair to Bass, even after she weakened it, the program has still resulted in more than 7,700 affordable apartments under construction, according to her campaign.   Bass opposed SB 79, a landmark California law that passed in 2025 requiring cities and suburbs to allow construction of denser housing near transit stops
Permitting apartments near public transit is one of the most basic principles of sensible urban planning
But in LA, it was controversial enough that Bass urged Gov

After he signed SB 79 into law anyway, Bass worked with LA’s city council to delay much of the law’s most ambitious upzoning until 2030, while permitting smaller apartment buildings near some transit stops.  After the devastating January 2025 fires, some property owners whose homes had burned down in the Pacific Palisades had applied to rebuild under SB 9, another important California law that allows single-family lots to be modestly densified into up to four housing units

In response to backlash from some neighbors , Bass reportedly pressed Newsom to restrict SB 9 in fire-damaged areas; she then banned SB 9 applications in parts of the Palisades. (There are certainly legitimate questions about whether rebuilding in such a fire-prone area is a good idea at all

But Bass offered no publicly available analysis that the modest increase in density allowed by SB 9 posed a special danger, even as she worked to accelerate the rebuilding of single-family homes.)  All of these point to a leader who is not serious about changing the conditions that led to LA’s housing shortage, and lacks the courage to take on what is arguably the city’s most defining political challenge
Raman has promised to fundamentally break from that approach
That will make her mayoralty an important experiment for the rest of the country
Even modest progress in a city as resistant to housing as LA could help crack open a way forward for new approaches to housing in the many other cities that face affordability crises
This won’t be easy for her — she’ll face the same anti-building political pressures, and will need to maintain a cooperative relationship with the city council
When I spoke to Raman over the summer, I noticed that she treaded gingerly around the topic of adding density to single-family neighborhoods
Because of the uniquely American obsession with keeping single-family homes segregated from other types of development, it can be a real political third rail in LA and nationwide
But research has suggested the city can’t fill its housing shortage without building more in those neighborhoods

Raman will, at least, have an important ally in California’s newly elected governor, Xavier Becerra, who is also a strong YIMBY.  Raman’s affiliation with the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) makes her emblematic of a fusion that’s been emerging in Democratic politics, between supply-side abundance and left-wing economic populism
It’s also evident in politicians like Zohran Mamdani and some of the young Democrats who won elections across the country this week.  I think this is right
It's not just that Talarico (et al) combines elements of left populism, abundance pragmatism, and cultural moderation
It's also that the definitions of "left" and "moderate" are in flux

Take "left." Talarico's all-of-the-above position on energy, eg,… https://t.co/elbUP9vT11 — Derek Thompson (@DKThomp) November 5, 2026 From talking to Raman, I have the sense that she’s more at home with the YIMBY part of her politics than the DSA part
Her relationship with the DSA’s LA chapter has been strained (though it did endorse her candidacy)

But her social-democratic commitments are also sincere — she’s been a strong champion of rent control and tenant protections in LA, for example, and helped shape a stronger rent stabilization law the city adopted last year.  The new political syntheses taking shape on the American left are exciting and intriguing
Whether it will finally make a breakthrough in LA’s — and California’s, and America’s — housing crisis, of course, remains to be tested
But it’s a welcome sign that American politics need not remain trapped in the same orthodoxies and failures.

title: Trump wants an immigration deal. He could start with caregivers.
excerpt: Unlike projecting how many jobs AI may eliminate over the next 10 years, or what a country’s birth rate might look like, there’s far less debate among policymak
body: Unlike projecting how many jobs AI may eliminate over the next 10 years, or what a country’s birth rate might look like, there’s far less debate among policymakers about how large America’s older population will be in a decade’s time, and how many of them are likely to need direct care for disabilities
By 2036, as the baby boomers continue to retire, the US population 65 and older is expected to grow from 65.6 million to 77.5 million people, according to the Congressional Budget Office
The number of people 85 and older is also expected to nearly double in that time, from 6.8 million to 11.1 million
The question of whether the United States will have enough direct care workers — an umbrella term that refers to home health aides, personal care aides, and nursing assistants — looms large

These are workers, primarily women, who help older adults and people with disabilities bathe, dress, eat, take their medication, and generally get through a day, either in a nursing home or in someone’s own home

It’s a massive, often ignored workforce (the American Community Survey estimates there were 3.62 million of them in 2024) and it’s paid for largely by Medicaid, the joint federal-state health insurance program that most people associate with coverage for impoverished Americans but which is actually the dominant payer for long-term care in this country.  Key takeaways By 2036 the US will need 625,000 to 1.3 million more direct care workers, and policymakers across the aisle agree the demand is real and coming

Three bipartisan-friendly proposals — the Dignity Act, the Careworker Visa Act, and a Brookings caregiving visa — would bring in immigrant caregivers with built-in protections learned from past programs
With around 40 cosponsors from both parties and Problem Solvers Caucus backing, the Dignity Act has more bipartisan traction than most immigration bills in years
Trump has also expressed new openness to immigration reform

Depending on which researcher you ask, the US will need somewhere between 625,000 and 1.3 million additional direct care workers over the next decade to keep pace with the growing number of older and disabled Americans — and that’s just to maintain today’s level of care as the population ages, not to fix the shortage that already exists
If you’ve talked to anyone currently trying to coordinate long-term care, you probably already know the country is understaffed as it is

To close the gap, policy experts say the United States should bring more immigrants into a sector that’s already about one-third immigrant , while also protecting the roughly 12 percent of current direct care workers who are noncitizens, some of them undocumented

PHI, a national nonprofit that researches and advocates for the direct care workforce, projects 9.6 million direct care job openings between 2025 and 2035, the bulk of which will come from existing workers changing fields, retiring, or otherwise leaving the workforce. “We can’t do it with the current US-born workforce,” Amy Robins, the senior director of policy at PHI, told me. “We need to have mechanisms where people can come into this country and do this work.” Immigration reform has felt politically impossible in Washington for years, but after the brutal defeat Republicans suffered in the midterms, there’s a suddenly a much stronger case that this corner of the fight is different
Days after the election, President Donald Trump gave an interview saying his deportation policy was “too tough” and he’d be open to some sort of immigration reform deal to protect workers
Kevin Cramer (R-ND) and Dick Durbin (D-IL) reintroduced a bill to recover green cards that went unused in earlier years and redirect them to nurses and doctors

Coordinating care for older adults is a problem that reaches families in every corner of the country, and even comfortable households wonder whether they can secure a dignified life for an aging parent, or, eventually, for themselves

With family caregivers growing in number and nursing homes turning residents away because they can’t find staff, caregiving may be the one corner of immigration policy Congress is actually willing to fix

A growing menu of options Over the last year or so, three different proposals have emerged that suggest that caregiving is the immigration battle Washington is finally ready to fight.  In July 2025, Reps

María Elvira Salazar (R-FL) and Veronica Escobar (D-TX) introduced the Dignity Act , which pairs tougher border enforcement with legal status for undocumented immigrants who’ve been in the country since before 2021
It also offers permanent residency for Dreamers and a handful of green card reforms

Salazar herself has pitched the bill partly as a remedy for the same aging-population squeeze driving the caregiver shortage, and eldercare groups such as LeadingAge and the American Seniors Housing Association have thrown their support behind it .  The legislation rests on an idea at the center of the caregiving political fight, which is that immigration enforcement alone won’t get the US the labor it needs

Since then, the Dignity Act has gathered around 40 cosponsors, split nearly down the middle between the parties, and this spring it won the endorsement of the Problem Solvers Caucus, a group of roughly 60 members whose mandate is passing legislation both sides can live with

Following Trump’s recent comments that he’d be open to an immigration deal, Salazar praised him on X, urging him to throw his weight behind the Dignity Act. “You can surpass Reagan’s legacy by delivering a historic immigration reform,” she posted. “This is your moment.” There are other ideas on the table, too

Gabe Vasquez (D-NM) introduced the Careworker Visa Act , a bill that would create a new temporary visa allowing up to 100,000 immigrants a year to work in childcare, eldercare, and home-based disability care

It would also let some immigrants already living in the US obtain work authorization through the program and give participating workers a pathway to permanent residency. “We all know that immigrants are already taking on these jobs in large numbers,” Vasquez told me. “One of the conversations we’re having amongst the Democratic coalition is how to craft meaningful immigration-related legislation that can be bipartisan on a couple specific issues
And certainly this bill rises to the very top of that conversation.” And the most recent entry came in September, from Tara Watson, an economist at the Brookings Institution

In a new caregiving visa proposal , she offers the idea of a visa open to immigrants with at least two years of direct care experience who want to come to the US to work as home health aides, personal care aides, or nursing assistants
It would start at 30,000 visas a year before rising to 65,000 after three years, and employers would have to pay above-market wages and provide health insurance
Learning from what didn’t work Neither of the two dedicated caregiving visa proposals is starting from scratch
In 1999, Congress created a visa for nurses to work in understaffed hospitals, but the process had such strict eligibility rules that fewer than 15 hospitals nationwide ever qualified to use it
And it was burdensome for qualifying workers, too: If a nurse ever wanted to switch their hospital, they had to start their visa certification process all over again
Over the course of a decade, barely a thousand visas were ever issued, and lawmakers let the program expire in 2009.  Other countries have gone the opposite direction
The UK made care workers eligible for its Health and Care Worker visa in 2022 , and the numbers took off almost immediately, with 106,000 visas granted in 2023 alone

Some contracts required workers to repay thousands of pounds to their employer if they left before their visa term was up — one worker’s contract demanded more than 11,000 British pounds — which made leaving a bad job financially impossible for people who’d often already gone into debt just to get the job in the first place
More than 43,000 workers were affected when their employers’ sponsor licenses were revoked amid widespread reports of exploitation
The UK ended overseas recruitment for care workers in 2025, though the broader Health and Care Worker visa remains in place
Both experiments reflected the fact that workers often had no way out, no matter how poorly an employer behaved

Watson and Vasquez say they kept that front of mind when crafting their proposals, both of which allow workers to switch jobs rather than staying locked to whoever sponsored them.  “You really do see this tension — the more you try to make sure the workers are protected, the more onerous it becomes for the employers,” Watson told me. “You’re choosing between scale and some of those restrictions

I’m trying to hit somewhat of a middle ground.” Vasquez pointed to the H-2A visa program for farmworkers, which he said has also had real, ongoing problems with employers abusing the system.  “Anytime that we are creating new programs for immigrant workers in which their job status depends on them achieving legal status, we should always be aware that there may be bad folks that are seeking to abuse that system,” he told me. “That’s going to require some thoughtful support for the Department of Labor for enforcement of laws just like this.” States can’t fix this alone These federal ideas build on top of a patchwork of state-level attempts to raise direct care wages in order to incentivize more people living here to enter and stay in the field
Yet for all the state mandates, bonuses, and training programs, care programs are usually among the first casualties when money gets tight

title: Two cities just voted to get Flock cameras out. It’s only the beginning.
excerpt: An aerial view of a Flock camera on September 14, 2026, in Burbank, California. | Justin Sullivan/Getty Images As Flock cameras have quietly multiplied across t
body: An aerial view of a Flock camera on September 14, 2026, in Burbank, California. | Justin Sullivan/Getty Images As Flock cameras have quietly multiplied across the country in recent years, public concern about privacy, surveillance, and abuse of the technology by law enforcement has sparked nationwide backlash

This led to a number of cities pausing, not renewing, or canceling their contracts with Flock Safety, the leading company behind the controversial AI-enabled automated license plate readers, this year.  And now, citizens have voted on the issue.  Towns in two states, Texas and Maine, voted on midterm ballot measures concerning Flock

And in both cases, the people ruled against the tech.  While these are just two communities out of the thousands that use the cameras — hardly enough to dismantle the nationwide surveillance network — these results show the real possibility of taking on mass surveillance and winning

But one issue remains: Even if the initiatives that passed on Tuesday inspire similar civic resistance in future elections, the fight against the problem that Flock represents is just beginning for those who don’t want their every move tracked.  Nongovernmental entities — such as college campuses, homeowners associations, even supermarkets — have started purchasing and deploying Flock cameras of their own and sharing the data with law enforcement.  Now, the fight will need to go beyond the ballot box.  An end to the status quo? While some advocates for Flock systems argue that the company’s AI-enabled automated license plate readers (ALPRs) may make solving certain crimes easier, public attention has been drawn to overt misuse of the technology by current and former law-enforcement officers

Even some police leaders have expressed concerns about Flock’s ability to target people who have not been accused of a crime, potentially raising serious constitutional issues.  Both York, Maine, a small city of about 14,000, and the midsize League City, Texas, took the issue to the ballot box.  In York, residents were asked to consider a citizen initiative called the “ Stop ALPRs Ordinance ” that made the ballot after receiving over 100 residents’ signatures
Its residents decisively rejected the surveillance cameras, with 5,386 votes (73 percent of the vote) in favor of the ordinance and only 2,043 votes (27 percent) against
Effective immediately, the measure bans ALPRs in the town of more than 14,000 and requires voter approval before the town installs any such tech in the future

Meanwhile, in League City, Texas, voters decided on an advisory question, Proposition A , which asked: “As a nonbinding statement of voter preference, should the League City Police Department continue using automated license plate reader cameras at fixed locations on public roadways for law enforcement purposes?” Voting “yes” on the measure meant approving the use of ALPRs at fixed locations on public roadways for law enforcement purposes, while a “no” vote would oppose such uses
Though the ballot question was technically non-binding, League City’s City Council committed to act on the vote’s outcome

The measure passed with 54 percent of the vote.  In response to a request for comment about these two measures, a Flock spokesperson told Vox, “We’re grateful to both York and League City elected leaders and community members who engaged in this conversation

Flock technology has had a real impact helping to solve crime in those cities and across the country.” The company added, “While we’re disappointed in the outcome, we respect the decision voters made and will work directly with the city on next steps.” To privacy advocates working in the surveillance space, these wins signify a shift. “The status quo for the longest time has been that cities and law enforcement agencies have been able to approve and award massive contracts for surveillance tech and rarely have any sort of trouble passing them,” said Reem Suleiman of the digital rights group Fight for the Future , which advocates against mass surveillance and hosts the site StopALPRs.com. “In 2026, this isn’t the case.” “People feel and understand that they do actually have a stake when it comes to surveillance tech and how it’s used.” Reem Suleiman, Fight for the Future The backlash has been building for some time, Suleiman said, pointing to the nonprofit Secure Justice’s tracker of nearly 500 actions by cities over the past year to pause or terminate Flock contracts

She also noted that the fight has moved beyond city councils — a Senate Judiciary hearing in late September showed bipartisan interest in reining in license plate readers, and federal and state proposals are multiplying

Because these decisions to employ ALPRs and other surveillance technologies have typically been made without public input, Suleiman said, putting the question to voters reflects a meaningful change: “People feel and understand that they do actually have a stake when it comes to surveillance tech and how it’s used.” Voting against local city use of Flock cameras, however, may be just the tip of the iceberg.  Where the fight goes next The uptake of Flock cameras by nongovernment actors presents a separate accountability challenge that may complicate the efforts of anti-surveillance activists
Homeowners associations, hospitals, schools, and big retailers are contracting for the same technology, with no council meetings for citizens to pack and no ballots to vote on
According to reporting by Inc. , of the approximately 12,000 customers using Flock cameras, 5,000 are private-sector entities
These private buyers can opt to have the data generated by their cameras automatically shared with law enforcement
Many of them do just that, including commercial chains such as Home Depot and Lowe’s, and Simon Properties , the US’s largest network of shopping malls

According to Flock’s website , if these private customers choose to share data with local law enforcement, they can allow the system “to notify authorities when a flagged license plate is detected, without requiring action from the camera owner.” One of Fight for the Future’s current targets is Lowe’s, which Suleiman described as one of the largest commercial buyers of Flock cameras. “I don’t want anybody to live under a false sense of security because, unfortunately, there are so many different ways we are exposed to surveillance and to these cameras,” she said
Critics of license plate readers also fear that cities are swapping out one vendor for another without addressing underlying concerns about data privacy and surveillance

For instance, Axon, a $48 billion company that produces a slew of law enforcement technology, has capitalized on Flock’s recent PR challenges by swooping in to replace its competitor in at least seven municipalities across five states
In that context, even more ballot measures might not be enough to address the concerns of privacy advocates

Suleiman still has thoughts about what ordinary people can do to push back against increasingly privatized networks of surveillance technology.  “Get involved in those fights,” Suleiman said. “There is a lot of power that consumers have in terms of voicing their values and insisting from the places they shop and the brands that they love that they’re not going to be complicit in the surveillance network.”

body: Paul Mackenzie convicted over deaths of children and one adult after followers were ordered to starve themselves and their families The leader of a Kenyan doomsday sect has been sentenced to 200 years in prison for the murders of 190 children and one adult in one of the world’s worst cult disasters in recent history

title: ANC faces bruising defeat in South African local elections with 80% of ballots counted

body: Former liberation movement’s share of national vote almost 14 percentage points below 2021 result The African National Congress is on course to suffer a bruising defeat in South Africa’s local elections, with the once dominant party of Nelson Mandela falling to under a third of the vote nationally with more than 80% of ballots counted
Wednesday’s fragmented vote marks another stage in the decline of the ANC, which has led national governments since the end of white minority apartheid rule in 1994
High unemployment, crime, corruption and poor local service delivery have all contributed to voters turning away from the party

title: The Download: a humanoid cleans house and Samsung builds for the AI boom

body: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology
I watched a humanoid robot clean my apartment
It felt like a taste of the future. —Grace Huckins When I saw an X post about a new humanoid-robot cleaning service in San Francisco, I immediately signed up for the waitlist
I wanted my apartment to feel like The Jetsons , even if just for an hour
The device that arrived at my building belongs to Tau Robotics, a local startup
Its long-term goal is to make autonomous cleaning robots a reality, but the technology isn’t quite there yet
For now, humans pilot the robots remotely, watching them work through onboard cameras
There were some unexpected challenges along the way, but also moments that felt like a glimpse of the future
Find out how well the machine cleaned my home—and how close we are to truly autonomous domestic robots
A visit to Samsung’s massive new semiconductor hub Generative AI models depend on stacks of specialized memory chips
To meet soaring demand, Samsung is building a vast new semiconductor manufacturing campus in Pyeongtaek, South Korea
I visited the sprawling campus south of Seoul, where three fabs already operate around the clock, a fourth is coming online, and thousands of workers are racing to build a fifth
Step inside the vast chipmaking complex powering the AI boom . —Michelle Kim This story is from the Impossible edition of our print magazine
